The correct answer is B (Snap rings together with strap and bolt retainers depending on yoke design): heavy duty universal joint yokes typically retain the bearing caps with either internal or external snap rings seated in a groove, or with a strap and bolt design where a formed strap clamps the cap in place with bolts torqued to specification. Using the wrong retention method can allow a bearing cap to walk out under load.
  13. The correct answer is A (Angular velocity fluctuation, which is also sometimes called non-constant velocity motion): whenever a single universal joint operates at an angle, its output shaft speeds up and slows down twice during every full revolution of the input shaft, even though the average speed matches. This fluctuation is what a properly phased two joint driveshaft is designed to cancel out between its two ends of the shaft.
  14. The correct answer is C (Disconnecting one driveline at a time and road testing to see which change matters): removing or disconnecting one driveline at a time, where safely possible, and re-testing lets the technician confirm which shaft is contributing to the vibration, since eliminating the true source will change the symptom while eliminating an unrelated component will not. This process of elimination is standard practice for tandem drive train diagnosis.
  15. The correct answer is D (Approximately one to three degrees, always confirmed against manufacturer specification): most heavy truck driveline manufacturers specify that the angles at each end of a single joint driveshaft should be within about one to three degrees of each other to keep the resulting velocity fluctuation and vibration within an acceptable range. Angles that exceed this tolerance produce a torsional vibration that grows worse with road speed as the truck accelerates.
  16. The correct answer is B (That poorly applied weights may detach at speed or indicate improper prior balancing): factory and professional shop balancing uses precisely placed and securely welded or bonded weights confirmed on a balancing machine, and crude field additions raise doubt about whether the shaft was actually brought back into proper balance. A weight that detaches at highway speed can itself introduce a sudden new vibration or become a road hazard for other drivers.
  17. The correct answer is B (A systemic change in driveline operating angle caused by the ride height modification): when the same modification precedes an identical symptom on two separate trucks, the shared variable, the ride height change, is far more likely the cause than coincidental component wear occurring independently. Lowering ride height changes the geometric relationship between the transmission and the axle, which directly alters driveline operating angles at both ends of the shaft.
  18. The correct answer is C (A single driveshaft runs directly from the transmission output shaft to the axle pinion): on a straight truck with a single drive axle, one driveshaft assembly with universal joints at each end and typically a slip joint connects the transmission output shaft to the axle's pinion input. This is simpler than a tandem tractor arrangement, which requires an additional inter axle driveline and power divider.
  19. The correct answer is C (Replace the plugged fitting, or the whole joint, so lubrication can resume): a plugged grease fitting means the internal bearing surfaces are no longer receiving fresh lubricant, which accelerates wear and eventually causes the clicking or knocking symptoms associated with a dry joint. Replacing the fitting, and inspecting whether the internal cross passages are also blocked, restores proper lubrication practice going forward.
  20. The correct answer is B (It significantly reduces the resulting torsional vibration transmitted through the entire driveline): when the angles at each end of the shaft are equal and opposite, the velocity fluctuation created by one joint is largely cancelled by the fluctuation created by the other, producing much smoother power delivery. This is the entire reason manufacturers specify matched angle tolerances rather than only a single maximum angle figure.
  21. The correct answer is B (Correcting the driveline geometry with an angle kit or a double Cardan joint): repeated premature universal joint failure at otherwise normal mileage strongly suggests the joints are operating outside their designed angle tolerance, so replacing worn joints with the identical part will produce the same accelerated failure again. Correcting the underlying geometry, or upgrading to a double Cardan joint rated for a steeper angle, addresses the actual cause of the wear.
  22. The correct answer is D (The driveshaft is bent or damaged and should be replaced rather than reused): excessive runout at the centre of the tube means the shaft is not rotating on a true, straight axis, which is almost always the result of a bend from impact, improper handling, or a manufacturing defect. A bent driveshaft cannot be trusted to run smoothly at any speed and will produce vibration that gets worse as road speed increases.
  23. The correct answer is C (The flat, machined ear surfaces of each yoke aligned in the same rotational plane): properly phased yokes have their bearing cup ears aligned in the same plane so that both universal joints bend in a coordinated way as the shaft rotates through an angle together. Technicians visually confirm this alignment, or rely on factory index marks, when assembling or reassembling a two joint driveshaft correctly.
  24. The correct answer is B (The suspension ride height and the resulting driveline operating angles under load): as load increases, the rear suspension compresses and the ride height at the drive axle changes, which alters the pinion angle relative to the transmission output angle. This kind of isolated finding lets the technician target the repair to the correct component.
  82.   87. This has no effect on transmission gear selection, the engine brake, or steering assist, which are all unrelated systems.   89. The correct answer is B (Tractor B will show measurably greater wear inside the power divider and inter axle set): Repeatedly leaving the inter axle lock engaged during normal driving, including on dry pavement where axle speed differences occur constantly, forces the inter axle gearing and power divider to resist that natural speed variation far more often than appropriate use on genuine low traction surfaces would ever require. It does not reverse rotation direction, does not change either axle's internal gear reduction ratio, and does not redirect all torque to one axle exclusively, since both axles still receive drive torque, just now at a forced matching speed.
  92. This kind of hands on confirmation is a reliable way to validate the mechanism during a scheduled inspection.
  93. The clutch design, the presence of universal joints, and the engine itself are not fundamentally changed by adding a tandem configuration.   94. The clutch brake, the transmission auxiliary calibration, and steer axle alignment are unrelated to a power divider gear whine and would not explain this specific symptom appearing right after this specific repair.   95. The correct answer is B (Torsional windup builds through components not designed to routinely absorb it while cornering): Because a locked differential prevents the natural speed compensation needed between the inside and outside wheels through a turn, the resulting resistance builds torsional stress, or windup, through the axle shafts and gearing, components that are not designed to routinely absorb that kind of load during normal cornering. This risk has nothing to do with engine idle speed, turbocharger boost, or the transmission being forced into neutral, none of which are affected by axle lock status. Recognizing this windup risk is central to understanding why the lock is restricted to low traction use only.
  96. The correct answer is B (Gather driver details on the noise, then isolate and check backlash before disassembly): Starting with a detailed driver description of when the noise occurs, followed by isolation techniques such as disconnecting the inter axle driveline and checking gear backlash with a dial indicator, allows the technician to narrow the fault to a specific carrier before any disassembly begins, saving significant labour and avoiding unnecessary parts replacement. Immediately tearing into both differentials, replacing the entire assembly, or defaulting to a clutch adjustment without evidence all skip the systematic process that properly targets the actual fault. This ordered approach reflects the whole system thinking described for tandem drive train diagnosis.
  97. The correct answer is D (It must receive the correct gear oil at the specified interval, like any other carrier): Like any other gear carrier on the truck, the power divider and inter axle differential housing holds its own gear oil and must be serviced at the manufacturer's recommended interval to prevent premature wear, since it is a separate housing from the engine crankcase and is not a sealed, maintenance free unit. It does not share sump oil with the engine, and it does not use the same fluid that operates the pneumatic range and splitter shift cylinders, which is compressed air rather than any liquid. Routine gear oil service is essential to the assembly's long term durability.
  98. The correct answer is D (It has an additional power divider and inter axle differential the single axle lacks): The core difference in drive train complexity comes down to the additional gear sets, specifically the power divider and inter axle differential, that exist purely because of the tandem configuration and have no equivalent in a single drive axle straight truck. The engine, tire compound, and transmission gear ratio count are not inherently different simply because a truck is built with a tandem rather than a single drive axle. This additional gearing is exactly why tandem drive trains require the extra diagnostic steps discussed for isolating a fault.
  99. The correct answer is C (It only spans the short distance between two closely spaced tandem axles): The inter axle driveline only needs to bridge the relatively short distance between the two tandem axles, whereas the main driveline has to span the much longer distance from the transmission all the way back to the forward axle, and this physical distance is simply what determines each shaft's length. The inter axle driveline still carries significant torque and operates at a comparable rotational speed to the main driveline, so neither of those factors explains the length difference, and overall weight reduction is not the design intent behind this particular shaft's length.
  100. The correct answer is D (The rear axle receives no drive torque at all until the driveline is reconnected): Since the inter axle driveline is the only physical path carrying torque from the power divider back to the rear axle, disconnecting it completely removes drive torque from that axle until the shaft is reconnected, which is precisely why this disconnection is a useful diagnostic isolation technique. The inter axle lock alone cannot supply torque without the driveline in place, the rear axle has no alternate direct connection to the transmission, and there is no electrical torque path in this mechanical drive train. This is strictly a temporary diagnostic step, not a normal operating condition.
  101. The correct answer is A (Frequent low traction turning likely increases both legitimate and mistimed lock engagement): A gravel quarry environment naturally involves more frequent low traction surfaces and tight manoeuvring, which increases both the frequency of legitimate lock engagement and the risk of the lock being engaged or left on during turns where it should not be, both of which place extra wear and shock loading on the power divider and inter axle gearing over time. Fuel contamination and elevation related horsepower loss are not plausible mechanisms for concentrated power divider wear specifically, and dismissing the environmental connection outright ignores the clear operational pattern the foreman has observed.
  102. The correct answer is C (Locking stops the spider gears from rotating relative to the case, removing the noise): When the inter axle lock engages, it bypasses the differential action entirely, so the spider gears stop rotating relative to the differential case even though torque is still flowing through the assembly, which removes the very motion that was generating the wear related whine in the first place. Locking the differential does not change oil flow, does not meaningfully reduce the torque passing through the housing, and has no relationship to engine ignition timing. Recognizing that the lock can mask a differential gear noise is an important diagnostic insight.
  103. The correct answer is C (The lock collar teeth briefly struggling to engage due to a slight axle speed difference): If the two tandem axles are turning at even a small speed difference the instant the lock is commanded, the collar teeth may momentarily struggle to fully engage, producing a brief surge, hesitation, or clunk felt by the driver before the collar seats completely. A slipping clutch disc, a brake system air leak, and a restricted fuel filter are all unrelated mechanisms that would not produce a symptom tied specifically to the moment of inter axle lock engagement. This is why proactive, low speed engagement is recommended over engaging the lock after a speed mismatch has already developed.
  104. The correct answer is B (Locks should generally be engaged only at low speed and disengaged once traction returns): The correct guidance for both the inter axle lock and the tandem axle differential lock is that they should be engaged only when needed at low speed on low traction surfaces and should be disengaged again as soon as normal traction returns, since sustained use at higher speeds or during turning increases the risk of component damage. Locks are not intended for continuous use at highway speed, they do not automatically disengage based on transmission gear position on most conventional systems, and they have no functional relationship whatsoever to cruise control. This written guidance reflects standard manufacturer recommendations for lock use.
  105. The correct answer is A (Combining housings reduces the number of separate mounts, seals, and shafts on the chassis): Integrating the power divider into the forward axle carrier reduces the overall number of separate housings, mounting brackets, and driveline sections the manufacturer would otherwise need if the power divider were a completely separate mid chassis unit, simplifying the design and reducing weight and complexity. There is no technical reason a stand alone unit could not physically split torque between two axles, the housing still absolutely requires gear oil regardless of its location, and there is no blanket regulation against a mid chassis mounted unit. Packaging efficiency is the more reasonable explanation.
  106. The correct answer is C (The forward axle wheels lose all drive torque, since the power divider is their only path): Because the power divider is the single point that receives torque from the main driveline and feeds it into the forward axle's own differential, a complete internal failure that stops torque transfer through the power divider will also stop torque delivery to the forward axle's wheels, not just to the rear axle. There is no direct mechanical path from the engine flywheel to the forward axle wheels bypassing the power divider, and there is no automatic backup torque routing from the rear axle in a conventional mechanical drive train. This illustrates why the power divider is such a critical single point in the tandem torque path.
  107. The correct answer is D (The two axles rotate at slightly different speeds matching the different arc radii travelled): With the inter axle differential unlocked and functioning correctly, the forward and rear axles should be free to rotate at slightly different average speeds as the truck follows a circular path, since each axle traces a slightly different arc radius through the turn, similar in principle to how the two wheels on a single axle rotate at different speeds through a corner. Both axles rotating at exactly identical speeds during a turn would actually suggest the differential is not functioning, and either axle remaining completely stationary would indicate a serious drive train fault rather than normal operation.
  108. The correct answer is C (A standard one allows two wheels to differ in speed, an inter axle unit allows axles): Both devices apply the same underlying differential gear principle, but a conventional differential applies it between the left and right wheel of a single axle, while an inter axle differential applies that same principle one level up, between two entire drive axles in a tandem set. Neither device directly increases horsepower or fuel economy on its own, standard differentials are found on drive axles generally rather than exclusively on steer axles, and neither device is hydraulically or purely electronically operated in a conventional heavy truck drive train.
  109. The correct answer is C (Both tandem axles would show accelerated, irregular wear, similar to constant manual lock use): A seized, permanently locked inter axle differential produces the exact same forced speed matching between the two tandem axles that occurs whenever the lock switch is manually engaged, and since that condition would now exist continuously rather than only in low traction situations, the resulting scrubbing and accelerated, irregular tire wear on both tandem axles would occur constantly rather than occasionally. Tire wear would not improve under this condition, the steer axle is unaffected by the tandem's inter axle differential, and the differential's status very much does influence how the tandem tires interact with the road during every turn.
  110. The correct answer is B (Improper timing or surface conditions when engaging it can shock load expensive components): Because engaging the inter axle lock at the wrong time, such as during a turn on dry pavement or after wheel spin has already begun, can shock load and damage the collar, the power divider gearing, or the inter axle differential itself, drivers need to understand it is a functional mechanical device with real consequences rather than a simple convenience switch. The switch is not cosmetic, misuse carries genuine mechanical risk beyond just a warning light, and its function has no dependency on which transmission gear is currently selected. Proper driver education on this point can prevent costly repairs.
  111. The correct answer is A (Clutch, transmission, main driveline, power divider and inter axle set, then the rear axle): Torque leaves the engine and passes through the clutch into the transmission, then travels down the main driveline to the power divider inside the forward axle, where the inter axle differential allows the split portion of torque to continue rearward through the inter axle driveline into the rear axle's own differential and finally out to the wheels. Any sequence that places the clutch after the transmission, or the power divider before the clutch and transmission, misrepresents the actual mechanical order torque must follow through this system. Understanding this order is fundamental to systematic drive train diagnosis.
  112. The correct answer is B (A dial indicator measuring ring and pinion backlash against the manufacturer's specified range): A dial indicator is the correct tool for measuring the small clearance, or backlash, between the ring gear and pinion teeth inside the power divider, and comparing that reading against the manufacturer's specified range tells the technician whether wear has progressed beyond an acceptable limit. A multimeter, an air pressure gauge, and a feeler gauge for clutch lining are all tools intended for entirely different systems and would provide no useful information about internal gear mesh condition inside the power divider.
  113. The correct answer is D (Continuing normally with the lock still engaged on regained good traction risks windup): Once good traction returns, the natural small speed differences between the two axles resume, and if the lock remains engaged the axles are still forced to match speeds exactly, producing the same windup and wear risk discussed for driving locked on dry pavement in general. Leaving the lock engaged does not by itself store a transmission fault code, does not affect engine warm up, and has no relationship whatsoever to the vehicle's legal gross weight rating. Disengaging the lock promptly after conditions improve is simply good practice to protect the drive train.
  114. The correct answer is C (More frequent legitimate and occasionally mistimed lock use increases overall wear exposure): Winter mountainous service naturally presents far more genuine low traction situations calling for lock use, and with more frequent engagement comes a statistically higher chance that some engagements happen at less than ideal moments, such as slightly mismatched axle speed or a patch of unexpectedly better traction encountered mid turn, both of which add up to greater overall wear exposure on the power divider and inter axle gearing over the life of the truck. Cold temperature does not meaningfully shrink properly designed gear teeth, grade changes can absolutely affect axle loading and traction demand, and there is no indication a different part number is used based on climate alone.
  115. The correct answer is B (Both together are acceptable only in the most severe low traction cases at low speed): While many trucks are mechanically capable of having both the tandem axle differential lock and the inter axle lock engaged simultaneously for the most extreme low traction situations, this combination should still be limited to low, straight line speed for the same fundamental reason either lock alone requires that caution, namely the risk of severe windup if turning or speed mismatch occurs while everything is locked. It is not universally forbidden on every truck, it has no effect on available horsepower, and simply being at maximum gross weight does not by itself require using both locks.
  116. The correct answer is D (Raise the wheels, disengage the lock, and confirm one axle can rotate independently by hand): Rotating one tandem axle by hand while the wheels are safely raised and the lock is disengaged should allow the other axle to remain stationary or turn independently at a different rate if the inter axle differential is functioning correctly, giving a direct physical confirmation that the rebuilt gear set properly allows speed compensation. A dash light illuminating at ignition merely confirms a bulb and circuit work, shift cylinder air pressure relates to an unrelated transmission function, and clutch pedal return has nothing to do with the power divider. This hands on check is the most direct way to confirm the repair was successful.
  117. The correct answer is D (A recirculating ball gear, using a worm shaft riding on circulating ball bearings): Heavy trucks almost universally use recirculating ball steering gears rather than rack and pinion units common on cars. Inside the gear, ball bearings circulate through a track to reduce friction and multiply steering effort at the sector shaft. This design tolerates heavier loads and rougher service far better than a passenger car style gear. The sector shaft output ultimately drives the pitman arm and the rest of the linkage.
  118. The correct answer is A (It is splined to the pitman arm and outputs the gear's rotary motion): The sector shaft is the output shaft of the recirculating ball gear and is splined directly to the pitman arm. As the worm shaft rotates, the sector shaft converts that motion into the output that swings the pitman arm. The pitman arm then converts rotation into linear motion carried through the drag link to the knuckle. This handoff is the core mechanical path through the entire steering gear.
  119. The correct answer is A (The Ackermann principle, coordinated through the tie rod between the two knuckles): The Ackermann principle describes the correct proportional relationship between inside and outside front wheel angles, since the inside wheel turns a tighter arc. The tie rod connects the left and right knuckles so both wheels turn together while keeping this proportion correct. Without proper Ackermann geometry, the front tires would scrub sideways during every turn and wear rapidly. This principle governs steering geometry, not suspension or driveline components.
  120. The correct answer is C (A vane type pump, driven off the front of the engine by a belt): A vane type pump is the standard hydraulic source for heavy truck power steering, driven off the front of the engine by a belt or gear train. It draws fluid from a reservoir and delivers it to the control valve built into the gear housing. Because the pump is engine driven, its output changes with engine speed, which the gear's valving is built to manage. Other pump types listed here are used for unrelated systems on a heavy truck.
  121. The correct answer is B (A torsion bar mounted inside the steering gear housing itself): A torsion bar inside the gear twists a small amount whenever the driver applies steering effort. That twist opens internal passages directing pressurized fluid to one side of a power piston in the housing. The piston then assists the worm shaft's movement, cutting the physical effort needed to steer a heavily loaded axle. The pitman arm and drag link are downstream linkage parts, not the sensing element for driver input.
  122. The correct answer is B (Dual steering gears joined by a coordinating shaft between the primary and slave gear): Some heavy trucks with higher front axle ratings use dual steering gears to handle the added load. A second, slave gear mounts further back on the frame and links to the primary gear by a coordinating shaft. This splits the mechanical load across two gear sets rather than asking one gear to carry the whole steer axle. It is a load sharing design, not a backup or redundancy system.
  123. The correct answer is A (About seven and one eighth inches of free play measured at the rim before the front wheels begin to respond at all): CVSA and Transport Canada out of service criteria for a power steering equipped commercial vehicle define excessive gear lash in inches of movement measured at the steering wheel rim, scaled to the wheel's diameter, not in degrees of rotation. For an 18 inch diameter power steering wheel, the published limit is about seven and one eighth inches of rim travel before the front wheels begin to respond. A technician checks this by rocking the wheel gently while watching the pitman arm for lost motion. Lash beyond this limit is an out of service condition because it degrades driver control and response time.
  124. The correct answer is B (By grasping the joint and trying to move it against its non pivoting direction): A technician checks a ball joint, tie rod end, or drag link end by grasping it and trying to move it in a direction it is not built to pivot in. A healthy joint shows no perceptible motion in that direction. Any detectable movement points to internal wear, and a torn dust boot is treated as its own separate defect. This hands on check is distinct from the gear lash procedure done at the wheel.
  125. The correct answer is D (Fluid that has turned dark in colour and carries a distinct burnt smell): Dark, burnt smelling power steering fluid is a recognized sign of internal wear generating excess heat inside the pump or gear. Healthy fluid stays relatively clear and free of a burnt odour through its normal service interval. Once it darkens and smells burnt, internal parts are already suffering accelerated wear from that heat. A technician finding this should investigate the pump and gear rather than simply topping up fluid.
  126. The correct answer is D (The drag link running between the pitman arm and the left knuckle): The drag link is the linkage member running from the pitman arm, the gear's output, to the steering arm on the left knuckle. From there the tie rod connects both knuckles so the wheels turn together in correct proportion. The torque rod and equalizer beam are suspension components controlling axle position and load sharing, not steering linkage. Knowing this chain from gear to knuckle is basic to diagnosing linkage looseness.
  127. The correct answer is A (A second drag link carrying motion back to the rear steer axle): On trucks with tandem steer axles, a second drag link carries steering motion back from the front linkage to the second axle so both turn in coordination. This keeps the rear steer axle tracking correctly through every turn instead of fighting the front one. Without this link, tandem steer axles would scrub tires and produce unpredictable handling. This differs from a dual steering gear, which splits effort rather than coordinating a second axle.
  128. The correct answer is B (Worn joints there can add play and affect overall steering feel and response): The steering column uses one or more universal joints carrying rotation from the wheel down to the gear input, often routing around cab obstructions. Wear in these joints can add play and affect how precisely driver input reaches the gear. This is separate from the gear lash check performed at the pitman arm. Fluid overheating, camber problems, and tire cupping trace instead to the pump, alignment, and suspension.
  129. The correct answer is A (Built directly into the steering gear housing alongside the torsion bar): The control valve directing pressurized fluid to the power piston is built into the steering gear housing, working with the torsion bar. This lets the valve respond immediately to the torsion bar's small twist as the driver applies effort. The pump's job is simply to feed pressurized fluid to this valve, not to control its direction. Keeping the valve in the gear housing minimizes lag between driver input and assist.
  130. The correct answer is D (Gear lash exceeds the common out of service limit and needs correction): about eight inches of rim travel before the pitman arm responds exceeds the commonly cited seven and one eighth inch threshold for an 18 inch diameter power steering wheel, so this lash is excessive and out of service. This test isolates lash inside the gear, separate from looseness at the tie rod ends or drag link. A worn gear allows this extra play because internal parts, such as the worm and sector shaft engagement, have worn past tolerance. The finding points toward gear adjustment or replacement.
  131. The correct answer is B (The joint should be moved against its non pivoting direction, not its designed axis): A ball joint or tie rod end pivots freely along its intended axis, so checking movement there proves nothing useful. The correct method grasps the joint and tries to move it against the direction it is not built to move in. Testing the wrong direction can produce a false pass on a joint with real internal wear. This is a simple but easily confused point in steering linkage inspection.
  132. The correct answer is A (The condition and tension of the belt driving the power steering pump): A slipping or worn belt reduces the vane pump's speed and output, cutting the pressure and volume available for assist even with normal fluid level and colour. This matches the symptom described, since belt slip has the greatest relative effect at low engine RPM. Camber, height control valves, and tire date codes belong to alignment, ride height, and tire aging instead. Checking the belt is a logical, inexpensive first step.
  133. The correct answer is D (Yes, since perceptible play against the non pivot direction is a defect by itself): Perceptible movement against a joint's non pivoting direction is a defect on its own, no matter the dust boot's condition. The boot only keeps contamination out and grease in, so an intact boot just means the joint stayed protected from the elements. A joint can still wear internally through normal fatigue even with a perfect boot. Both a torn boot and measurable play stand as independent defects each requiring documentation.
  134. The correct answer is C (The condition and adjustment of the shaft coordinating the two steering gears): A coordinating shaft physically links the primary and slave gear so both share the steering load evenly. If that shaft loosens or falls out of adjustment, the two gears can fight each other, producing feel that would not exist on a single gear truck. The tie rod, height control valve, and tire age exist on either configuration and are not unique to a dual gear check. This question targets what changes once a second gear is added.
  135. The correct answer is A (Test the pump's actual output pressure and flow against factory specification): If a belt swap does not fix high steering effort, the pump may be internally worn and unable to produce enough pressure or flow even when driven correctly. Testing pump output against specification isolates the pump from a downstream fault such as the gear's valve or piston. Replacing the whole gear without this test risks an unnecessary and costly repair. Toe setting and tire pressure affect handling and wear, not gear assist.
  136. The correct answer is C (As a defect, since a torn boot allowing contamination in stands on its own): A torn dust boot is a defect on its own, since it lets dirt, water, and road debris contaminate the joint even before any looseness appears. Waiting for measurable play to develop before flagging the boot would catch the fault only after damage begins. Regreasing does not stop the ongoing contamination path a torn boot creates. Mileage has no bearing on whether a torn boot must be documented.
  137. The correct answer is A (The right side steering linkage and tie rod ends for binding or damage): The pump and its internal control valve normally supply assist evenly regardless of turn direction, so a one sided heaviness or pull points toward mechanical binding or damage on that side. A bent tie rod or a seized joint on the right could explain a symptom isolated that way. The pump and torsion bar are shared, symmetric parts unlikely to cause a purely one sided effect. Trapped air tends to cause noise or overall inconsistency, not a directional pull.
  138. The correct answer is A (The tie rod length and its two connection points at the steering knuckles): The tie rod links the two knuckles and sets the proportional relationship between inside and outside wheel angles, the mechanical basis of Ackermann geometry. If that proportion is wrong, tie rod length or its attachment points are most likely to need adjustment. The height control valve, pump belt, and torsion bar all serve different systems with no bearing on turning angle proportion. A scrubbing complaint therefore starts at the tie rod linkage.
  139. The correct answer is C (The steering column universal joints and their connection points along the column): The gear lash test isolates play inside the gear itself but does not evaluate wear in the column universal joints between wheel and gear. Worn column joints can add a vague feel to driver input before it even reaches the gear. Frame section modulus, suspension air pressure, and hub end play are unrelated to how driver input travels down the column. This tests recognizing that a feel complaint can start upstream of the gear.
  140. The correct answer is D (An internal fault in the gear's control valve or piston causing uneven assist): With pump, belt, and fluid all confirmed correct, the remaining likely cause sits inside the gear, such as a valve or piston not distributing assist evenly by direction. That kind of internal wear can create a directional imbalance even with a fully normal hydraulic supply. Power steering has no electrical dependency on the alternator here, ruling that out. Overinflation and a cracked rail would each show different symptoms, not a direction specific effort change.
  141. The correct answer is C (Document the loose splined connection as a defect that needs correction): Play at the splined pitman arm to sector shaft connection is a serious defect on its own, since it means gear output motion is not reliably reaching the linkage. This connection should be inspected and torqued or replaced to specification, since it is a known failure point on heavy trucks. Ignoring it leaves the truck with unpredictable steering response under load. Tightening the unrelated tie rod clamp bolts would not correct play at this joint.
  142. The correct answer is D (The fitting could work loose in service even after being torqued correctly): A cotter pin or lock nut is secondary retention meant to stop a castellated nut from backing off under vibration a steering linkage sees in service. Correct torque alone does not guarantee the fastener stays tight over thousands of kilometres, which is why secondary retention is specified. Omitting it creates a real risk the fitting loosens even after being correctly torqued. This has no direct effect on gear lash, pump pressure, or the opposite tie rod.
  143. The correct answer is B (Rocking the steering wheel while watching only the pitman arm for lost motion): Watching the pitman arm while the wheel is rocked isolates play inside the gear, since any wheel motion before the arm responds must occur inside the gear itself. Checking tie rod and drag link ends instead tests the linkage downstream of the gear. Toe measurement and fluid condition are useful for other complaints but do not isolate gear lash specifically. This distinction between gear lash and linkage lash comes up often on inspections.
  144. The correct answer is B (Pump output depends somewhat on engine speed, which is often lower during yard work): Because the pump is driven off the engine, its output relates to engine RPM, and yard work often pairs lower RPM with large steering inputs at low speed. That combination can make assist feel weaker relative to the effort tight turns demand. The gear has no road speed cutoff for providing assist, and neither the tie rod nor torsion bar change behaviour with vehicle speed. A marginal pump can make the effect worse.
  145. The correct answer is B (The pump's internal condition, using a proper flow and pressure test): External checks such as belt tension, fluid, and visible leaks can all look correct even with a pump that has lost real output pressure and flow internally. A flow and pressure test against factory specification is the only way to confirm the pump's actual internal condition. Caster affects self centering and directional stability more than baseline effort, tire age affects tread, and the equalizer pivot is a suspension part with no bearing on steering effort.
  146. The correct answer is C (It lets the slave gear tie into the linkage at a separate load sharing point): A slave gear mounts further back specifically so it can tie into the linkage at a separate point, sharing the mechanical load of steering a heavy front axle rather than concentrating it at one gear. This placement is purely about load distribution, not proximity to the fifth wheel, engine heat, or the suspension height control valve, all unrelated systems. The coordinating shaft keeps primary and slave gear working together despite the separation.
  147. The correct answer is B (A whining pump noise along with inconsistent or jerky steering assist): Trapped air in a hydraulic power steering circuit is a known cause of pump whining or groaning along with jerky, inconsistent assist as air compresses instead of solid fluid moving through the system. Bleeding after any service that opens the circuit is required to remove this air. Gear lash, frame bending, and torsion bar failure are unrelated mechanical conditions and would not follow simply from skipping the bleed step. This is a common comeback after a pump swap.
  148. The correct answer is B (Reduced pump output at low RPM combined with a pump that is already marginal): Because pump output ties to engine RPM, a marginal pump may meet demand at higher RPM but fall short at idle, giving a symptom that tracks directly with engine speed. This pattern points to the pump struggling to hold flow and pressure at low RPM rather than a structural or linkage issue. A cracked rail or torn boot would not correlate specifically with idle speed. Camber changes wear and pull, not RPM dependent effort.
  149. The correct answer is D (Its ball bearings travel a track and continuously return to the start of it): The word recirculating describes how the ball bearings travel a track around the worm shaft and are guided back to the start of it as the shaft turns, rather than rolling along a fixed path once. This recirculation lets the balls keep cutting friction through continuous rotation rather than running out of track. It has no relation to the power steering fluid, pitman arm output, or the tie rod, all separate parts.
  150. The correct answer is D (Air is entering the system, possibly through a loose suction hose or low level): Milky, aerated hydraulic fluid is a classic sign of air entering the circuit, often through a loose suction hose fitting or a reservoir level that drops enough to expose the pickup under dynamic conditions. This differs from water contamination, which produces a different, thicker appearance more common in lubricating oil systems. A disconnected drag link would cause an obvious, immediate loss of steering control instead. Aeration should be fixed at its entry point, not just topped up.
  151. The correct answer is A (Document the reading as within spec and recheck it at the next scheduled visit): A reading right at the limit, without exceeding it, should be documented accurately and treated as passing for now, since the standard exists to define where the line sits. Because wear tends to progress, flagging it for closer attention at the next scheduled inspection is reasonable rather than ignoring it entirely. Replacing a gear that is within specification is an unneeded repair the measurement does not support. The torsion bar has no bearing on mechanical lash readings.
  152. The correct answer is C (Truck B, since splitting the load across two gear sets eases each individual gear): Dual gears exist specifically to share a heavier steer axle's mechanical load across two gear sets rather than concentrating it in one gear, which for equal axle load can lower the demand on each gear and ease steering effort. A single gear handling the same load alone gets no such sharing benefit. Tire pressure affects rolling resistance and handling but is not the main factor in gear generated assist. Dual gear layouts respond to load, not cost alone.
  153. The correct answer is B (Caster angle, which provides a truck's self centering tendency after a turn): Caster angle specifically drives a vehicle's self centering tendency, so insufficient caster produces exactly this complaint, a wheel slow to return to center even with normal turning effort. This is an alignment characteristic rather than a hydraulic assist issue, so pump belt tension and internal gear lubrication would not typically create this specific symptom. A wheel seal is a sealing component entirely unrelated to return behaviour. Correcting insufficient caster through shims or bushings addresses this symptom directly.
  154. The correct answer is D (A pressure and flow test using a gauge set connected into the hydraulic circuit): A pressure and flow test, run with the correct gauge set per manufacturer procedure, confirms a pump's actual output under real load conditions. Visual checks such as belt condition, fluid level, and cap integrity cannot reveal internal pump wear that lowers pressure or flow. Timing a manual wheel rotation with the engine off gives no meaningful data on hydraulic assist. Steer axle tread depth affects traction and wear, not pump hydraulic output.
  155. The correct answer is C (The steering linkage and tie rod ends on that side, at full steering lock): A click occurring only at full lock in one direction commonly points to interference, wear, or looseness in the linkage or a joint reaching the end of its travel on that side. Belt slip usually produces a squeal or whine, not a distinct click, and would not be isolated to one direction of lock. The rear equalizer pivot and height control valve sit far from the front linkage and would not produce a noise tied to steering wheel position.
  156. The correct answer is B (The arm could be installed out of index, so the wheel no longer sits centered): Many pitman arm and sector shaft connections include an index mark ensuring only one correct rotational position relative to the gear's centered point. Skipping this check can leave the steering wheel off center with the wheels pointed straight ahead, even with a correctly torqued fastener. This misalignment is purely positional and has no direct effect on pump pressure, internal bearings, or the frame rail. Index alignment must always be verified during a pitman arm reinstall.
  157. The correct answer is D (The power steering pump bearing and drive belt for a developing fault): A failing power steering pump bearing commonly produces a growling noise that tracks engine and pump speed, and can also reduce assist as the pump's internal condition worsens. This combination points at the pump and belt rather than the steering gear, which sits away from the engine and does not typically produce RPM linked noise. The height control valve has no engine speed relationship, and a cracked crossmember typically ties to road load, not engine RPM.
  158. The correct answer is B (Integrating the piston lets assist act right on the worm shaft under load): In the recirculating ball design the power piston sits inside the gear housing so assist acts on the worm shaft right where mechanical resistance is highest, keeping assist efficient and directly coupled to effort. This integrated design still needs a torsion bar to sense driver input and control the valve, regardless of piston location. The pump is still required to feed pressurized fluid to the piston either way. The pitman arm still links the gear output to the drag link in either layout.
  159. The correct answer is D (Weak or inconsistent assist even though pump, belt, and fluid all look normal): A relief valve stuck open lets fluid bypass back to the reservoir instead of building assist pressure, giving weak or inconsistent assist that is hard to trace since the pump, belt, and fluid all look correct externally. This is an internal hydraulic fault rather than mechanical wear, so it would not show up as rising gear lash, a frame crack, or a toe change, none of which connect hydraulically to the relief valve. A pressure and flow test is usually required to diagnose it.
  160. The correct answer is A (An off centre pitman arm can leave the wheel crooked and cut travel in one direction): A recirculating ball gear has a specific internal centered point, and reinstalling the pitman arm while the gear sits off centre can leave the wheel crooked at straight ahead while also reducing travel available in one direction. This is a functional and safety concern, since reduced travel could limit the ability to complete a tight turn. The centering step applies whether the truck uses a single gear or a dual gear arrangement, not just one configuration.
  161. The correct answer is D (Excessive gear lash found during the standard steering wheel rock test): Excessive gear lash found at the gear is a steering system finding, since it means the gear allows more free play than intended before wheel response, producing exactly the wandering feel described at highway speed. A leaking air bag, worn equalizer bushing, or failed bounce test are all suspension findings that could also affect tracking but repair through the suspension, not the gear or linkage. Separating these systems correctly avoids repairing the wrong component for a wandering complaint.
  162. The correct answer is C (Trapped installation air is settling out and fluid is filling the space it occupied): A slight apparent level drop right after a pump swap is common as trapped installation air works out of the system, letting fluid fill the space that air occupied, a normal part of bleeding. A true manufacturing defect venting fluid would usually be visible as an external leak, not just a level shift. The recirculating ball gear does not consume fluid as part of normal operation, and the torsion bar has no fluid drawing function.
  163. The correct answer is A (Internal mechanical friction inside the gear, such as a worn track or binding shaft): With pump output already confirmed correct, excessive steering effort at the wheel points toward internal mechanical friction inside the gear itself, such as a damaged ball track or a worn worm shaft dragging even correct hydraulic pressure down. The height control valve belongs to the air suspension circuit and has no hydraulic tie to power steering. Tire load range affects capacity, not baseline effort, and frame section modulus is a structural bending rating unrelated to gear friction.
  164. The correct answer is A (Wheel and tire balance and roundness on the steer axle): A speed dependent, rhythmic wheel pulse with nothing found inside the steering system is a classic sign of an out of balance or out of round steer axle tire or wheel, since imbalance transmits periodic force back through the linkage. Fluid colour relates to pump wear and heat, not a pulsing feel. Torsion bar preload affects assist response, not a speed correlated pulse, and drag link length affects toe rather than producing a rhythmic feel.
  165. The correct answer is D (Wheel alignment, particularly camber and thrust angle, since a pull can start there): With the entire linkage already confirmed sound from tie rod ends to gear lash, a pull is often traced to alignment, particularly uneven camber or an incorrect thrust angle pushing the truck slightly off centre. Belt tension affects overall assist level, not directional pull, since the gear's control valve supplies both directions equally. Column joint phasing and internal gear lubrication are unusual, non standard explanations for a pull and are not the recognized path once linkage is cleared.
  166. The correct answer is D (Internal drag somewhere in the gear or column resisting the natural centering motion): Since caster is the main geometric driver of self centering and is already confirmed correct on both trucks, a slow return in spite of correct geometry points to internal drag somewhere in the gear or column resisting the motion correct caster should produce. Assuming the rack is miscalibrated ignores that the measurement was already confirmed and ignores an equally plausible mechanical cause. Tire pressure is a secondary factor at best, and drag link length mainly governs toe, not return speed.
  167. The correct answer is C (The coordinating shaft between the two gears adds a connection point where wear accumulates): A dual gear system adds a mechanical connection point, the coordinating shaft, that simply does not exist in a single gear setup, and any extra connection is another spot where wear or play can accumulate over time. There is no inherent reason dual gear systems use lower quality parts, since they are chosen for load demands, not cost cutting. Both layouts keep a torsion bar at each gear, and dual gear layouts are chosen by axle rating, not exclusively by off road use.
  168. The correct answer is A (Yes, since Truck B's sudden onset should prompt a wider check for other impact damage): Even with identical measured lash, the mechanism behind it differs. Truck A's gradual wear over years of normal use fits a straightforward gear and linkage inspection. Truck B's sudden onset right after a hard pothole impact should raise concern for other impact damage, such as a bent tie rod, damaged drag link, or frame damage near the steering system, all worth checking before simply correcting the lash. Treating both cases identically risks missing hidden damage on Truck B.
  169. The correct answer is C (A slow internal seal leak can consume fluid without a puddle while signalling other wear): A slow internal leak, fluid passing an internal seal rather than escaping outward, can steadily consume fluid with no visible puddle, and the same seal wear often signals other internal components are also beginning to wear. This links the seemingly separate observations of repeated top ups and later pump or gear failure through one underlying cause. Fluid in a sealed system does not evaporate fast enough to explain frequent top ups, a clogged vent would more likely cause pressure buildup, and repeated overfilling would not reliably correlate with later wear.
  170. The correct answer is C (Off road routes add far more shock loading and contamination exposure than smooth highway driving): Off road and construction routes expose linkage joints to far more shock loading from rough terrain, plus more dirt and debris that can work past seals even under a compliant schedule, both of which speed up wear compared to smooth highway driving. Nothing suggests off road trucks use a different gear design, since the difference lies in operating conditions, not architecture. With the schedule identical across both groups, it is not the most likely explanation. Steering frequency alone does not account for the gap without shock loading and contamination in the picture.
  171. The correct answer is C (Treat it conservatively, document it clearly, and lean toward correcting given the stakes involved): Given that a steering failure at highway speed with a loaded vehicle is one of the most dangerous failures possible, a borderline reading right at the threshold is best treated conservatively, documented clearly, with a bias toward correction rather than passing on a technicality. Treating any at or below the limit as automatically fine ignores measurement variation and the real consequences of a failure. Relying only on driver feel discards an objective, repeatable measurement, and failing every disagreement automatically ignores the actual measured value and context.
  172. The correct answer is B (Gear lash measures free play and cannot by itself catch a part nearing fatigue failure): This shows that a gear lash check measures rotational free play, a completely different property from the accumulated fatigue stress that can eventually shear a part like a pitman arm, so a component can pass a lash check while quietly approaching fatigue failure that only a visual crack inspection would catch. This does not make gear lash checks useless, since they genuinely catch the wear type they are built for, but shows why other inspection methods should be paired with it. No single inspection at one point in time guarantees future condition over an extended stretch.
  173. The correct answer is D (The pump shaft and mounting bracket for wear, looseness, or a bent shaft): A wobbling pulley with correct belt tension points to a fault at the pump, such as a worn shaft bearing, a loose mounting bracket, or a bent shaft, any of which lets the pulley run out of true. The torsion bar, tie rod ends, and height control valve are unrelated and would not cause a visible pulley wobble at the pump. Left alone, a wobbling pulley can speed up belt wear and eventually damage the pump's own bearing further.
  174. The correct answer is B (Steering column joints, then gear lash, then the pitman arm and drag link, then tie rod): A logical sequence follows how driver input actually travels, starting at the column and its joints, moving through the gear and its lash, then out through the pitman arm and drag link, and finally to the tie rod and knuckles. Reversing this order, or starting at the pump, tires, or frame, does not match how steering input flows and can make a fault harder to isolate. The height control valve and equalizer pivot belong to the suspension, not a steering inspection sequence.
  175. The correct answer is B (Inside the steering gear itself or somewhere in the steering column above it): If rocking the tires by hand reveals no linkage play, the wheel's free play more likely starts further upstream, either inside the gear itself or in the column and its universal joints, neither of which this check would reveal. Tie rod end play is actually easier to detect with the tires off the ground, not harder, since it isolates linkage from tire and suspension motion. Wheel bearing play would typically show up, not hide, under this same check, and frame flex is a far less likely explanation.
  176. The correct answer is C (A heavy steer axle load would need impractically high gear ratios without hydraulic help): A heavy truck's steer axle can carry well over five thousand kilograms, and steering that load through mechanical advantage alone would need gear ratios so high the wheel would need far too many turns lock to lock. Hydraulic assist keeps a reasonable ratio while still keeping driver effort manageable at these loads. A recirculating ball gear can exist without power assist on lighter applications, so the two are not tied together. Column routing, not hydraulic assist, decides how many universal joints a column needs.
  177. The correct answer is C (Pump fluid feeds the gear's internal valve and piston, which assist the worm shaft): The pump's pressurized output goes specifically to the control valve and power piston built into the steering gear, which then assist the mechanical worm shaft driving the sector shaft, pitman arm, and linkage out to the wheels. A conventional recirculating ball gear system has no hydraulic cylinders built into the front hubs, and the pump has no connection to tire inflation. The air brake system is a separate pneumatic system with no hydraulic tie to power steering effort.
  178. The correct answer is A (The pitman arm or gear was reinstalled slightly out of its correct centered index): With no alignment work performed, an off centre wheel right after a steering repair most likely traces to the pitman arm or gear being reinstalled slightly out of its correct centered index. The pump supplies pressure symmetrically through the gear's shared valve and does not create a side specific pressure difference. Ball bearings in a properly working gear circulate continuously and do not migrate to one side. A backwards torsion bar would typically cause a far bigger functional problem than a simple centering offset.
  179. The correct answer is C (The heavier fluid is likely too viscous when cold, briefly straining the pump until it warms): A fluid heavier than specified can be noticeably more viscous at cold temperatures, briefly straining the pump to draw and move it until normal operating temperature thins it back out, which fits a whine that fades as the truck warms. This does not indicate every affected pump is near failure, since the pattern correlates with the fluid change and cold starts rather than random timing. A torsion bar is a mechanical valving component and would not react specifically to fluid viscosity in this way. A frame crack would not produce a symptom that fades predictably with temperature.
  180. The correct answer is A (Not entirely, since gear lash tests free play but not internal binding or valve related issues): A passing gear lash test rules out excess mechanical free play inside the gear, but it does not test for internal binding, an uneven control valve, or other faults that could still contribute to a wandering feel without producing measurable lash. Concluding the gear is completely fault free overstates what this one test actually measures. Ruling out Theory One this way also does not automatically prove Theory Two, since the equalizer bushing still needs its own direct inspection. Gear lash and wandering are related, so the test is relevant, just not exhaustive.
  181. The correct answer is A (Correct the gear lash now, and replace the dust boot before contamination causes real internal wear): Gear lash beyond the accepted threshold is a genuine out of service safety condition and needs correcting now, not later. The torn boot has not yet caused measurable play, but delaying it invites contamination that will accelerate wear and eventually produce a real, more expensive defect, so replacing it proactively is the more cost effective long term choice. Calling the gear lash cosmetic ignores its real safety implications. Waiting for the boot to fail before acting trades a cheap preventive fix for a more expensive reactive one later.
  182. The correct answer is B (C-channel profile, with a web and top and bottom flanges): Heavy truck frame rails are almost always formed into a C-channel cross section, consisting of a vertical web with a flange along the top and bottom. This shape provides excellent resistance to bending loads while keeping the rail's overall weight reasonable for the vehicle. A fully boxed rail is heavier and more costly to manufacture and is reserved for specialty applications. The C-channel shape also allows an inner liner rail to be bolted or riveted inside it for extra strength on vocational trucks.
  183. The correct answer is C (The rail's resistance to bending under an applied load): Section modulus is an engineering measurement of a frame rail's resistance to bending, based on its cross sectional shape and dimensions. Vocational trucks that carry off road loads or mount cranes need a higher section modulus frame to resist the extra bending stress those applications place on the chassis. A higher section modulus rail is often paired with a reinforcing inner liner rail for even greater strength. Section modulus is unrelated to weight per metre, crossmember count, or fifth wheel torque rating.
  184. The correct answer is D (To reinforce the main rail and increase its resistance to bending): An inner liner rail is bolted or riveted inside the main frame rail specifically to add strength and increase section modulus in areas that see higher bending loads, such as under a mounted crane or heavy vocational body. It adds weight rather than saving it, and it is a structural reinforcement, not a routing channel or a fifth wheel mounting surface. Liner rails are common on off road and heavy vocational applications where the standard rail alone would be inadequate.
  185. The correct answer is B (They concentrate stress and are common origin points for fatigue cracks): Bolt holes, bracket attachment points, and any hole drilled into the rail for an accessory all create stress risers in the steel, meaning load is not spread evenly and cracks tend to start there under repeated flexing. This is why a poorly placed aftermarket hole is specifically called out as a common crack origin point. Rust, VIN stamping, and painting are unrelated to why these locations receive this scrutiny. A technician who understands stress concentration knows exactly where to focus a visual and physical frame inspection.
  186. The correct answer is C (The vehicle is generally an out of service condition until repaired): A frame crack that extends more than about one third of the rail's height is a serious structural defect and is generally considered an out of service condition, since it threatens the integrity of the entire chassis. Painting over a crack does nothing to address the underlying structural weakness and would hide a serious defect. Delaying the repair or simply monitoring the crack risks it propagating further under normal driving loads. This threshold is one of the clearest pass or fail measurements applied during a frame inspection.
  187. The correct answer is D (A frame condition that is generally an out of service defect): A frame that is visibly bowed, sagging, or twisted so the vehicle no longer sits level is a structural defect, most often caused by overloading or a collision, and is generally treated as an out of service condition. Frame steel does not simply flex back into shape once permanently bent, so removing the load will not correct the sag. This is a structural safety issue, not a cosmetic one, and tire pressure alone could not cause a visibly bowed rail. The vehicle needs a proper inspection and repair before returning to service.
  188. The correct answer is D (Welding can create a heat affected zone that embrittles the steel): Frame rail steel is often heat treated, and welding directly on a highly stressed rail introduces intense localized heat that can weaken the surrounding material through heat affected zone embrittlement, making the area more likely to crack again. A bolted splice plate spreads the repair load across a wider area without altering the steel's temper. The choice has nothing to do with welding equipment capability or drivetrain warranty terms. Cracks are typically stop drilled first to prevent further spreading before the splice plate is installed.
  189. The correct answer is B (Racking, the frame twisting that crossmembers are designed to resist): Racking describes the tendency of the two parallel frame rails to twist relative to one another under uneven loading, and crossmembers such as K-braces, tubular members, and box section members are installed specifically to tie the rails together and resist this twisting. A loose crossmember reduces the frame's ability to resist racking and should be repaired promptly. Camber, feathering, and cupping are all terms describing wheel alignment or tire wear conditions and have nothing to do with frame twisting.
  190. The correct answer is D (A fifth wheel that fails to lock on the kingpin is immediately dangerous): A fifth wheel that does not lock correctly onto a trailer's kingpin can allow the trailer to separate from the tractor while underway, which is an immediately dangerous condition. Checking the locking jaws for proper engagement is therefore one of the most safety critical parts of a chassis inspection. Fuel economy, brake release timing, and fifth wheel height adjustment are unrelated to whether the locking mechanism secures the kingpin. Mounting bolts and the plate itself are also checked, but the locking function carries the greatest immediate risk.
  191. The correct answer is D (The attachment point has experienced repeated movement and fastener wear): An elongated, oval shaped rivet hole is a sign that the joint has been loose for some time and has experienced repeated small movements, gradually wearing the hole out of round. This is exactly the kind of defect a frame inspection is designed to catch, since a loose crossmember attachment reduces the frame's ability to resist twisting and can worsen quickly. Original manufacturing holes are round and properly sized, and elongation is not caused by thermal expansion of the steel. Loose or missing rivets and elongated holes must both be documented and repaired.
  192. The correct answer is A (The specific location along the frame and the loads it must resist): Manufacturers choose among crossmember styles such as the K-brace, the tubular crossmember, and the box section crossmember based on where along the frame the member sits and what loads and racking forces it needs to resist at that point. A crossmember near the rear suspension may need different strength characteristics than one near the cab mounts. Paint colour, tire brand, and fifth wheel type have no bearing on crossmember style selection. A replacement crossmember must match the original style and location requirements.
  193. The correct answer is B (It alters driveline angles by changing the alignment of the axles): Because the axles, suspension, and driveline are all mounted to the frame, a permanent twist changes the geometric relationship between the transmission, driveshaft, and axle pinion, which can alter driveline operating angles enough to produce vibration. This is one of the less obvious consequences of frame damage a technician must consider when a vibration complaint does not trace back to an obvious driveline component. Frame twist is unrelated to tire pressure, and while it can also affect steering, it is not limited to steering feel alone.
  194. The correct answer is B (Thoroughly inspect the crack's extent and document it for repair): Any crack found at a spring hanger bracket, a specific high stress location called out for extra scrutiny during a frame inspection, must be fully evaluated for length and depth and documented so a proper repair, such as stop drilling and a splice plate, can be planned. Painting over the area or tightening bolts does nothing to address a structural crack and can hide the true extent of damage from future inspections. Surface rust alone is common, but a crack at this critical location cannot be dismissed as routine.
  195. The correct answer is C (A cracked fifth wheel plate is a defect requiring repair or replacement): The fifth wheel plate carries the full weight of the loaded trailer and transmits kingpin loads to the frame, so any crack in the plate itself is a structural defect regardless of the locking mechanism's condition, and it must be repaired or the fifth wheel replaced before the vehicle returns to service. A crack in this load bearing component is a concern regardless of size. Field welding a bead over a cracked plate is not an acceptable repair for this safety critical component. Locking mechanism function and plate integrity are separate inspection points that must both pass.
  196. The correct answer is A (Material placed furthest from the neutral axis best resists bending): In any beam, including a frame rail, material located furthest from the neutral axis contributes the most to resisting bending, which is why flanges sit at the extreme top and bottom of the C-channel rather than near the middle. This principle is exactly what gives a C-channel rail its strength to weight ratio for resisting the bending loads a frame experiences. Flange location has a real structural purpose, it is not simply an appearance choice, and tires never mount directly to the frame rail flanges.
  197. The correct answer is D (Uneven ground would introduce false readings into frame measurements): If a truck sits on an uneven or sloped surface, the frame can appear out of level or misaligned simply because of the ground beneath it, producing false readings and leading to an incorrect diagnosis. Starting a frame straightness check on a known level surface removes this variable so any measured discrepancy can be attributed to the frame itself. This principle mirrors the requirement that alignment work be performed on a level rack. Skipping level ground checks could result in unnecessary and costly frame repairs based on faulty data.
  198. The correct answer is C (Overload damage tends to be a gradual sag, collision damage more localized): Chronic overloading typically produces a gradual, distributed sag or bow along the frame's length as the steel slowly deforms under repeated excess weight, while a collision tends to produce a more sudden, localized bend or crack concentrated near the point of impact. Recognizing this difference helps a technician form an initial hypothesis about the cause and likely extent of frame damage before beginning detailed measurements. Neither cause reliably produces sharp, localized bends every time, and the two damage patterns are often distinguishable rather than identical.
  199. The correct answer is A (They tie the two frame rails together and resist twisting forces): Beyond serving as mounting points, crossmembers exist primarily to tie the two parallel frame rails together across the width of the vehicle and to resist the frame twisting, or racking, as the vehicle travels over uneven ground or carries unbalanced loads. Different crossmember styles, such as K-brace, tubular, and box section designs, are chosen for this structural role based on where they sit along the frame. Ground clearance, driveshaft clearance, and rivet count are not the core purpose of a crossmember.
  200. The correct answer is A (Retorque or replace the loose bolts to the correct specification): Loose fasteners at a crossmember attachment point, whether bolts or rivets, are a defect that must be corrected, since a loose joint allows movement that concentrates stress and can lead to elongated holes and eventual cracking. The correct response is to retorque the bolts to specification or replace them if damaged, not to leave them loose or remove them and rely on the rivets alone. Both bolts and rivets at a given attachment point are typically load sharing fasteners, so all of them must be secure.
  201. The correct answer is C (The crack can propagate under repeated flexing and worsen before then): A frame crack, especially one that begins at a stress concentration point like a bolt hole, tends to grow under the repeated flexing and vibration a truck experiences in normal service, so a crack judged minor today can become a serious structural defect well before the next scheduled service. This is why every frame crack found during an inspection must be documented and evaluated rather than deferred. Washing has no effect on crack propagation, and there is no safe minor size below which a crack can simply be ignored.
  202. The correct answer is A (It allows the spring to lengthen slightly as it flexes under load): As a leaf spring flexes under a bump or a load, its effective length changes slightly, and the swinging shackle at one end accommodates this change so the spring is not fighting a fixed mounting point on both ends. The fixed hanger at the opposite end anchors the spring solidly to the frame. A shackle does not lock the spring rigid, has no role as an electrical ground path, and caster is adjusted through shims or tapered bushings, not the shackle. Worn shackle bushings are a common source of poor tracking.
  203. The correct answer is B (An equalizer, sometimes called a rocker, on the tandem suspension): The equalizer, also called a rocker, is a pivoting beam used on walking beam and four spring tandem drive axle suspensions to distribute load evenly between the front and rear drive axles even when the road surface differs under each one. This component, along with the torque rods that hold the axles in position, is central to how a tandem suspension shares load. A drag link and sector shaft belong to the steering system, and a torsion bar belongs to the power steering gear.
  204. The correct answer is C (They locate the axle and control driveline angle under torque): Torque rods on a tandem drive axle suspension hold the axle in its correct fore and aft position and resist the axle's tendency to rotate, or wind up, under driving and braking torque, which keeps driveline angles correct. Worn torque rod bushings allow the axle to shift position slightly under torque, a common cause of driveline vibration and unusual tire wear. Torque rods do not carry the vehicle's weight, which is the spring's job, and they have no connection to air lines or wheel speed sensor wiring.
  205. The correct answer is D (Poor tracking, uneven tire wear, and driveline vibration): Worn spring pin and equalizer bushings allow the axle to move slightly out of its intended position under load, which produces poor tracking down the highway, uneven or accelerated tire wear, and driveline vibration as driveline angles shift with the loose components. These bushings must be checked for looseness during a suspension inspection precisely because of these consequences. Worn suspension bushings have no connection to fuel economy improving, the parking brake, or tire inflation pressure, and none of those outcomes would result from this defect.
  206. The correct answer is B (Use a pry bar to check for movement between the pin and eye): With suspension weight relieved, a pry bar applied between the spring eye and the hanger bracket allows a technician to feel and observe excessive play in the pin and bushing, similar to how other suspension and steering pivot points are checked for looseness. This targeted check directly evaluates wear at that specific pivot. Tire tread depth, power steering fluid level, and fifth wheel jaw engagement are valid inspection points elsewhere but reveal nothing about wear in a spring eye bushing.
  207. The correct answer is D (Reduced spring capacity and load support on that corner): A leaf spring's total load carrying capacity comes from the combined stack of individual leaves, so when one leaf fractures completely, the remaining leaves must carry more of the load than they were designed for, which typically causes the corner to sit lower and produces the clunking noise as the broken leaf shifts under travel. This is not something the remaining leaves can fully compensate for, and it does not increase ground clearance or improve ride quality. A broken leaf spring should be replaced rather than left in service.
  208. The correct answer is A (Greater simplicity, durability, and lower cost in harsh conditions): Leaf spring suspension remains common on vocational and off road trucks specifically because of its mechanical simplicity, ruggedness, and lower cost compared to air ride, qualities that hold up well in the harsh, high impact conditions of quarry or construction site work. Air ride offers superior highway ride quality, a constant frame height, and the ability to be dumped for coupling, but those advantages matter less for a vehicle that spends most of its time off road. Fleet buyers weigh these tradeoffs against the vehicle's actual duty cycle.
  209. The correct answer is B (The U-bolts, spring pins, and shackle bushings for that corner): Before concluding a leaf spring has failed, a technician should verify the U-bolts securing the spring to the axle are properly torqued and that spring pins and shackle bushings are not so worn that they allow the axle to sit lower than it should. A loose U-bolt or badly worn bushing can create a sag symptom that looks like a spring problem but is really a mounting or wear issue. Windshield wipers, coolant level, and mirror adjustment have no connection to a suspension ride height complaint.
  210. The correct answer is D (The mating surfaces can settle slightly, reducing initial clamping force): When a leaf spring, axle seat, and U-bolts are newly assembled, the mating surfaces can compress and settle slightly under the first real driving loads, which can reduce the initial clamping force even though the bolts were torqued correctly at installation. Rechecking and retorquing after a short break in period, similar to the re-torque interval used after wheel installation, ensures the clamping force is still correct. This settling has nothing to do with U-bolt material expanding from heat or the paint applied to the spring.
  211. The correct answer is C (It anchors the spring and transmits all suspension loads to the frame): The spring hanger bracket anchors the fixed end of the leaf spring and transmits the full range of suspension loads, including bumps, braking, and acceleration forces, directly into the frame rail, which is exactly why it is one of the specific high stress locations called out for extra inspection scrutiny along with crossmember attachment points.
