A cracked, loose, or elongated hanger bracket can allow the spring end to shift position, degrading ride and tracking, or eventually failing outright. This bracket is one of the specific high stress attachment points a technician should never treat as routine.
  212. The correct answer is A (It aligns the spring leaves and axle so the assembly cannot shift sideways): The center bolt passes through all the leaves in the stack and its head locates into a matching hole in the axle seat, which keeps the spring leaves aligned with each other and correctly positions the spring relative to the axle before the U-bolts clamp everything together. It is not designed to carry the vehicle's weight on its own, that load is carried by the clamping force of the U-bolts and the leaves themselves. It has no connection to air ride height control or steering linkage.
  213. The correct answer is D (Loss of lubrication between leaves, increasing inter leaf friction): Multi leaf springs rely on a small amount of lubrication and controlled friction between the individual leaves to help dampen the spring's motion, but when the contact surfaces become dry and rusted, friction increases significantly, which stiffens the spring's action and produces both a harsher ride and an audible squeak as the leaves slide against each other. This condition has nothing to do with air springs, height control valves, or pressure protection valves, none of which exist on a leaf spring suspension. Anti-friction pads or spring lubricant address this wear pattern.
  214. The correct answer is A (Load sharing becomes uneven, allowing one axle to carry more weight): The equalizer's job is to allow load to be shared evenly between the front and rear drive axles of a tandem suspension despite small differences in road surface, and a worn pivot with excessive play undermines this function, allowing one axle to carry more than its intended share of the load at any given moment. This uneven load sharing contributes to accelerated tire wear and can affect braking and traction. A worn pivot does not improve load sharing, and it has no effect on the separate steer axle.
  215. The correct answer is D (The torque rod bushings that hold the axle in position): Even when an axle's own alignment angles measure correctly at rest, worn torque rod bushings can allow the axle to shift position slightly once the truck is under real driving and braking loads, which reintroduces incorrect toe or tracking dynamically and produces feathered tire wear that a static alignment check would miss. This is why a suspension inspection including torque rods and bushings is an important companion to any alignment check. The other listed components have no relationship to tire wear or axle positioning.
  216. The correct answer is C (Restricted spring flex, since the shackle end can no longer swing): A leaf spring's two ends are not interchangeable, since the fixed hanger end is designed to be rigidly anchored while the shackle end is designed to swing and accommodate the spring's change in length as it flexes. Installing the spring backwards would force the swinging function onto an end secured in a fixed hanger, restricting the spring's ability to flex properly and likely causing binding, harsh ride, and premature wear. This installation error would not affect braking function or tire size requirements directly, but it would compromise ride quality and spring life.
  217. The correct answer is B (It maintains a constant frame height and can be dumped for coupling): Air ride suspension is now standard on most highway tractors and many trailers because it delivers superior ride quality, maintains a constant, manufacturer specified frame height regardless of load, and can be dumped, or deflated, to make coupling and uncoupling a trailer easier. Air ride actually requires a dedicated air supply from the vehicle's air brake system, making it more complex and generally costlier than leaf spring suspension, not less. Shock absorbers are still used on air ride suspensions to control the oscillation of the air springs.
  218. The correct answer is D (Rigid trailing arms or torque rods connecting the axle to the frame): In an air ride suspension, the axle is located, meaning held in its correct position and controlled through acceleration and braking torque, by rigid trailing arms or torque rods rather than by the air springs themselves, which are only responsible for supporting weight and absorbing shock. The height control valve manages air pressure to maintain ride height but does not locate the axle, the pressure protection valve simply prioritizes air to the brakes, and the compressor generates system air pressure generally. Recognizing which component performs each of these roles helps a technician trace a suspension fault to its actual cause rather than guessing at parts.
  219. The correct answer is A (It ensures the air brake system always receives priority for available air): Because the air ride suspension draws its supply from the same compressed air system used for the vehicle's brakes, a pressure protection valve is installed in the line to guarantee the brakes always receive priority access to available air pressure, protecting braking performance even if the suspension circuit develops a leak or draws heavily on the system. This valve does not convert air to hydraulic pressure, filter moisture, or play any role in engine cooling. Its function is specifically about safeguarding brake air supply above every other air consuming system on the vehicle.
  220. The correct answer is C (It senses ride height and adds or exhausts air to maintain it): The height control valve continuously senses the frame's ride height relative to the axle through its linkage arm and either adds air into the air springs or exhausts air out of them as needed to maintain the manufacturer's specified ride height regardless of how the vehicle is loaded. This constant adjustment is what gives air ride suspension its ability to keep a consistent frame height whether the truck is empty or fully loaded. The valve has no role in tire pressure monitoring, engine idle speed, or driveshaft locking.
  221. The correct answer is B (The valve loses its ability to accurately sense actual ride height): The height control valve relies entirely on the mechanical linkage arm connecting it to the axle to sense the actual distance between the frame and the axle. If that linkage becomes disconnected, the valve can no longer accurately sense real ride height and will simply hold whatever air happens to already be trapped in the air springs, rather than actively correcting it, even though the valve and air lines themselves are functioning normally. This is a common cause of a truck sitting too high or too low on one corner.
  222. The correct answer is A (Driveline operating angles and headlight aim can both be affected): An incorrect ride height, whether too high or too low, changes the geometric relationship between the frame, the driveline, and the ground, which can alter driveline operating angles enough to cause vibration and can also change headlight aim enough to create a safety hazard for other drivers. At the extremes of suspension travel, incorrect height can also allow the air bags to be damaged by contacting the frame or axle. None of the other listed items, such as radio reception or mirror angle, are affected by ride height in this way.
  223. The correct answer is C (They dampen and control the oscillation of the spring): Shock absorbers are used on both leaf spring and air ride suspensions specifically to dampen and control the oscillation, or bouncing, of the spring after it is compressed by a bump, preventing the axle from continuing to bounce repeatedly. The air spring itself supports weight and cushions the initial impact but does little to control how quickly that motion settles without a shock absorber working alongside it. Shocks play no role in supplying compressed air, and toe angle is set through alignment adjustments, not by the shock absorbers.
  224. The correct answer is A (The corner returns to rest within about one or two oscillations): A properly functioning shock absorber should quickly dampen the spring's motion so the corner of the vehicle settles back to rest within roughly one or two oscillations after being pushed down and released. If the corner continues bouncing for many more oscillations, the shock absorber has lost its damping ability, often due to internal wear or a loss of hydraulic fluid, and should be replaced. A corner that does not move at all when pushed suggests something else entirely, not a properly working shock.
  225. The correct answer is C (Apply a soap solution around the seams and fittings, watching for bubbles): A soap solution applied around the air spring's seams, mounting fittings, and connections is a simple, effective way to visually pinpoint the exact source of a slow air leak, since escaping air will create visible bubbles at the leak point without requiring any disassembly. This is exactly the method used in a proper diagnostic approach before assuming the leak is coming from a specific component. Measuring compressor discharge pressure would not localize the leak, and replacing components based on a guess wastes time and money.
  226. The correct answer is B (It lowers the trailer height, making coupling and uncoupling easier): One of the practical advantages of air ride suspension is the ability to dump, or deflate, the air springs, which lowers the trailer to make it easier to align the kingpin with the fifth wheel during coupling or to separate the two units during uncoupling. This has nothing to do with increasing legal payload capacity, which is set by axle and tire ratings, and dumping the suspension does not disable the service brakes or convert the suspension type. Once coupling is complete, the height control valve restores normal operating height.
  227. The correct answer is B (The corner would ride noticeably too low compared to specification): If a height control valve becomes stuck in the exhaust position, it will continue venting air out of the air spring at that corner rather than holding or adding air, which causes that corner to settle progressively lower than the manufacturer's specified ride height. This is the opposite problem from a valve stuck in the fill position, which would cause that corner to ride too high instead. A stuck valve, in either direction, produces a real height change, and it has no connection to fuel economy at that corner.
  228. The correct answer is A (The suspension leak from draining air pressure needed for the brakes): The pressure protection valve exists specifically to prevent a leak or heavy draw anywhere in the suspension air circuit from draining air pressure away from the brake system, since braking performance must always be protected above the suspension's comfort and height functions. Even with a significant suspension leak, the valve keeps the brake circuit isolated and adequately supplied. A suspension air leak has no direct mechanical connection to headlight aim, the fifth wheel locking mechanism, or caster angle.
  229. The correct answer is C (The air spring can be damaged from rubbing against the frame or axle): Running at an incorrect ride height for an extended period pushes the air spring closer to the limits of its normal travel range, and at these extremes the air spring can be damaged by rubbing against the frame or the axle itself, potentially leading to a puncture or premature failure. This is one of the key reasons a stuck or maladjusted height control valve must be corrected promptly. An air spring does not self correct its own height, that is the height control valve's job.
  230. The correct answer is D (The height control valve, which continuously adjusts air spring pressure): The height control valve is the component responsible for maintaining a constant, manufacturer specified frame height regardless of how the vehicle is loaded, since it continuously senses ride height through its linkage arm and adds or exhausts air from the air springs as needed to hold that target height. The pressure protection valve only protects brake air supply and plays no role in height maintenance, shock absorbers dampen oscillation rather than carry static weight, and the drag link is part of the steering system entirely. This constant height feature is one of air ride's most valued advantages over leaf spring suspension.
  231. The correct answer is B (The right side air bag for leaks using a soap solution test): Following a methodical, system by system diagnostic approach, a technician who finds one corner sitting lower on an air ride suspension should first check that corner's air spring itself for a leak using a soap solution around the seams and fittings, since a leaking air bag is one of the most direct causes of a low corner. Only after ruling out a leak at the bag should the technician trace the air line back to the height control valve. Fifth wheel bolts, steering gear lash, and front tire tread depth have no bearing on this complaint.
  232. The correct answer is D (Trace the air line back to the height control valve and its linkage): When no leak is found directly at the air bag, the methodical next step is to trace the air line back to the height control valve serving that corner and inspect its linkage arm connection to the axle, since a loose or disconnected linkage rod prevents the valve from correctly sensing ride height even though the rest of the system functions normally. Replacing a component without confirming the actual fault wastes time and money, ending the inspection leaves a real defect unresolved, and checking the opposite side's tire pressure does not address this complaint. Confirming the actual fault before replacing parts is the more efficient and professional diagnostic approach.
  233. The correct answer is D (The corner runs on trapped, unregulated air instead of being actively maintained): With the height control valve's linkage disconnected, that corner is left running on whatever air happens to already be trapped inside the air bag, rather than having its pressure actively maintained and corrected by the valve as load and road surface change. This uncontrolled, unregulated condition produces both the low ride height and the harsher ride the driver described, since the air spring can no longer respond correctly to changing conditions. A disconnected linkage on one corner has no direct effect on the opposite side's air bag, on shock absorber operation, or on tire pressure.
  234. The correct answer is C (Verify correct ride height at that corner and complete a road test): After reconnecting the linkage rod, the technician should verify that the corner returns to and maintains the manufacturer's specified ride height, then complete a road test to confirm the harsh ride complaint has actually been resolved under real driving conditions. Returning the vehicle without confirming the fix risks sending it back out with the same complaint unresolved. Deliberately disconnecting the linkage again would recreate a known defect, and replacing an undamaged opposite side air bag as a precaution is not justified by the evidence found.
  235. The correct answer is A (It has failed and needs to be replaced along with the bushing): A shock absorber that is leaking oil from its body has lost its internal hydraulic fluid and can no longer generate the resistance needed to properly dampen suspension motion, and a torn or deteriorated mounting bushing further compromises how the shock is secured and how effectively it can do its job. Both conditions are recognized defects requiring replacement, and having both together makes replacement of the complete shock and its bushing the correct course of action. Shock absorbers are sealed units and are not designed to be topped up with fluid in the field.
  236. The correct answer is A (The core components serve the same functions, though details vary by axle count): Whether on a tractor's drive axles or a trailer's axles, air ride suspension relies on the same fundamental components performing the same functions, air springs supporting weight, trailing arms or torque rods locating the axle, a height control valve maintaining ride height, and shock absorbers controlling oscillation, though the specific number of axles and mounting details can vary between applications. Trailers absolutely use height control valves and do draw air from a supply line, and neither uses hydraulic springs, since this system relies on rubber air springs. Recognizing these shared functions helps a technician transfer diagnostic skills confidently between tractor and trailer air ride work.
  237. The correct answer is B (Air ride suspension, for its ride quality and consistent frame height): For a highway van trailer operating almost exclusively on paved interstate routes, air ride suspension is the better fit, since its superior ride quality helps protect freight, its constant frame height regardless of load simplifies coupling and handling, and it is already the standard choice for this exact type of application. Leaf spring suspension still requires regular maintenance of its own, and the dumping feature actually belongs to air ride, not leaf spring. Air ride does not eliminate the need for shock absorbers, since shocks still control the air spring's oscillation.
  238. The correct answer is C (Leaf springs are simpler, tougher, and less costly to repair if damaged): In a rugged, off road environment where suspension components risk impact damage from debris and rough terrain, leaf spring suspension's mechanical simplicity, durability, and lower cost make it a practical choice, since a damaged leaf or bushing is generally simpler and cheaper to repair than a punctured air spring or a damaged height control valve and its linkage. Air ride, not leaf spring, offers the dump and constant height features, and neither suspension type reliably offers a fuel economy advantage in every operating condition. Duty cycle and repair environment both factor heavily into this kind of fleet purchasing decision.
  239. The correct answer is B (The manufacturer's specified frame height dimension for that model): When adjusting or resetting a height control valve's linkage after service, the technician references the manufacturer's specified frame height dimension for that particular vehicle model, adjusting the linkage arm's connection point until the valve holds the axle and frame at the correct relative distance. Tire inflation charts, steering gear lash tolerance, and fifth wheel plate height are all legitimate specifications elsewhere in the vehicle's service data, but none of them are used as the reference for setting a height control valve's linkage. Getting this adjustment correct restores proper ride height, driveline angle, and headlight aim across the whole vehicle.
  240. The correct answer is B (A worn or failed shock absorber allowing the tire to oscillate): Cupping, the scalloped, evenly spaced dip pattern around a tire's circumference, points to a suspension or wheel end problem that allows the tire to bounce or oscillate repeatedly, and a worn or failed shock absorber that can no longer dampen spring motion is one of the most common causes of this specific wear pattern. The pressure protection valve only manages air priority to the brakes, the fixed hanger bracket belongs to a leaf spring suspension rather than air ride, and the drag link is part of the steering system. Recognizing this specific wear pattern lets a technician trace a tire complaint back to the true suspension cause without guessing.
  241. The correct answer is D (Checking shock absorber bounce test at each suspension corner): A failed shock absorber directly affects vehicle control and tire wear at highway speed by allowing the suspension to bounce uncontrolled after a bump, making the bounce test a genuine safety related check that belongs ahead of convenience items when time is limited. Radio operation and mirror alignment are driver comfort items with no direct bearing on vehicle safety, and reviewing rotation paperwork, while useful for planning, does not identify a current physical defect the way a hands on bounce test does. Prioritizing safety critical checks over convenience items is an expected professional judgment when a technician works under time pressure.
  242. The correct answer is D (It allows greater vertical travel while resisting excess lateral movement): A double convoluted, or reverse folding, air spring bellows is designed to allow a greater range of vertical suspension travel compared to a simpler single convoluted shape, while still resisting unwanted lateral, or side to side, movement of the axle relative to the frame. This design choice does not remove the need for a height control valve, which is still required to regulate air pressure and maintain height. An air spring, regardless of bellows design, does not replace the separate shock absorber's damping function.
  243. The correct answer is A (The suspension may be unable to maintain correct ride height): Since the air ride suspension draws its supply from the same compressed air system used for braking, a significant drop in overall system air pressure caused by a compressor fault can leave insufficient air available to the suspension circuit, even with the pressure protection valve prioritizing the brakes, meaning the height control valve may be unable to maintain correct ride height at one or more corners. This has no direct connection to frame cracking, steering gear power assist, which is generated by its own separate hydraulic pump, or wheel bearing temperature. Recognizing these interconnected systems helps a technician trace a suspension symptom back to its true root cause rather than treating it in isolation.
  244. The correct answer is C (Obtain the correct replacement air spring matching the original bolt pattern): An air spring's top and bottom mounting plates must match the original bolt pattern on the frame and axle bracket exactly, since these connections carry the vehicle's weight and must seal properly against air pressure, so a mismatched replacement should never be forced into service. Drilling new holes in the frame to accommodate the wrong part introduces unnecessary stress risers into a structural component, directly relating to the frame crack concerns discussed earlier, and oversized washers cannot safely compensate for a bolt pattern mismatch. The correct fix is always to source the properly matching replacement part rather than improvising a mismatched installation.
  245. The correct answer is B (Worn torque rod bushings allowing axle movement under torque): A clunk that appears specifically under hard acceleration, when driving torque is applied through the axle, points strongly to worn torque rod bushings, since the torque rods resist the axle's tendency to rotate or shift under torque, and worn bushings allow just enough movement to produce an audible clunk at that moment while remaining quiet at a steady cruising speed with no torque change. A height control valve issue relates to ride height rather than a torque driven clunk, and neither steer axle tire inflation nor a fifth wheel plate crack would produce this symptom. Recognizing this acceleration specific pattern helps a technician avoid unnecessary parts replacement elsewhere on the vehicle.
  246. The correct answer is C (It transmits axle location and driving loads directly into the frame): On an air ride suspension, the trailing arm pivot bracket performs a structural role similar to a leaf spring hanger bracket, since it transmits the axle's location forces and the driving and braking loads carried by the trailing arm directly into the frame rail, making it a genuine high stress attachment point that deserves the same thorough crack inspection. This bracket has nothing to do with air line routing and is a load bearing structural component, not a decorative one, so it should be included in a routine frame and chassis inspection. It should be included in every routine frame and chassis inspection rather than reserved only for a fifth wheel specific service interval.
  247. The correct answer is C (Camber, the tilt of the wheel viewed from the front): camber describes whether the top of the tire leans outward, positive camber, or inward, negative camber, when the vehicle is viewed head on. Excessive camber in either direction concentrates wear on one shoulder of the tire rather than across the full tread. Toe is instead measured front to rear across the axle, while caster and thrust angle describe entirely different reference planes. Recognizing which angle is being described is the first step before diagnosing a related tire wear complaint.
  248. The correct answer is D (Insufficient caster reducing the self centering tendency): caster gives a truck directional stability and helps the front wheels return to centre after a turn, and a vehicle with too little caster feels vague and wandering specifically at highway speed, where small steering corrections are magnified. Camber and tie rod length affect tire wear and tracking symmetry rather than high speed directional feel. A bent kingpin would typically produce binding or uneven effort rather than wander. Correcting caster is done through shims or tapered bushings at the axle mounting.
  249. The correct answer is A (Positive caster, which provides stronger straight line directional stability): heavy trucks are typically specified with slightly more positive caster than a passenger vehicle to counter their high centre of gravity and long wheelbase, improving straight line stability at highway speed. Negative camber is not a standard heavy truck steer axle setting since it would accelerate inner tread wear under normal loads. Toe out is not a target specification for highway steer axles, and thrust angle relates to rear axle tracking rather than caster's self centering function.
  250. The correct answer is B (Incorrect toe causing the tread ribs to feather): an incorrect toe setting causes the tire to scrub sideways slightly with every rotation even while travelling straight, which produces a feathered wear pattern with a sharp edge on one side of each rib and a rounded edge on the other. This tactile check lets a technician diagnose toe problems without needing an alignment rack. Underinflation and overinflation instead produce broad wear zones across the shoulders or centre, and a worn shock produces scalloped cupping rather than a feathered edge.
  251. The correct answer is C (The rear axle is not parallel to the front axle centreline): dog-tracking, where the vehicle travels slightly sideways or crabbed while appearing to go straight, results from a thrust angle problem, meaning the rear axle is not pointing straight ahead relative to the frame centreline. Uneven tire wear or a small toe drift on the steer axle typically produces a pull or wander rather than a visible crab angle. A slipping power steering belt affects steering effort, not the geometric tracking angle of the vehicle.
  252. The correct answer is C (Installing an offset bushing at the spring mounting): thrust angle problems on a spring suspension are commonly corrected by installing an offset bushing that rotates the axle slightly into correct alignment relative to the frame centreline. Tie rod ends affect steer axle toe rather than a driven axle's thrust angle, and height control valve adjustments and air pressure changes affect ride height rather than the rotational position of the axle housing on the frame.
  253. The correct answer is B (Confirming all tire pressures are set to specification): incorrect tire pressure alone can introduce enough measurement error to produce a false alignment diagnosis, so pressures are always confirmed correct before the vehicle goes on a level rack. Fuel level and mud flap removal have no meaningful effect on rack sensor readings. Building air pressure is necessary for the brakes and suspension to function normally but does not by itself correct a pressure related alignment error at the tires.
  254. The correct answer is D (Empty, with a full load of fuel and driver only): heavy truck alignment work is performed with the vehicle empty on a level rack, since a consistent, specified unloaded condition is what the manufacturer's alignment specifications are based on. Aligning under a partial or full load would change ride height and suspension geometry, producing a reading that does not match the published specification. This is separate from air ride height checks, which are also performed under a defined, specified condition.
  255. The correct answer is D (Toe out, with the front edges spread wider apart): toe out describes a condition where the front edges of a pair of tires are farther apart than the rear edges, the opposite of toe in, where the front edges are closer together. Camber and caster are entirely separate angles measured in a different plane and would not be the correct terminology for a front to rear tire spacing measurement. Accurately naming the condition matters because toe in and toe out are corrected in opposite directions.
  256. The correct answer is A (That wheel is running with excessive positive camber): wear concentrated on one shoulder with the rest of the tread wearing evenly, and with no feathered edge present, points specifically to incorrect camber on that wheel rather than a toe problem. Toe issues instead produce feathering across the full width of the tread, underinflation produces wear on both shoulders, and a worn shock produces scalloped cupping rather than a single-shoulder pattern. Eliminating feathering as a symptom is what isolates camber as the cause here.
  257. The correct answer is B (Dog-tracking, resulting from an incorrect thrust angle): a rear axle that is not parallel to the front steer axle's centreline produces an incorrect thrust angle, and the vehicle then travels crabbed, or dog-tracking, slightly sideways relative to its actual direction of travel. Bump steer describes a different problem where suspension travel changes toe geometry, and cupping describes a tire wear pattern rather than a directional tracking fault. Correctly naming the fault points the technician toward checking rear axle alignment rather than the front steering linkage.
  258. The correct answer is B (The direction the rear axle centreline points relative to the frame): thrust angle describes whether the rear axle or axles are pointing straight ahead relative to the frame centreline, and a misaligned thrust angle is what produces dog-tracking down the highway. Pitman arm travel and steering gear lash relate instead to the front steering system's mechanical condition, and axle housing tilt under load is a suspension deflection issue rather than a static alignment angle.
  259. The correct answer is C (Toe is measured front to rear, camber is viewed from the front): toe compares the distance between the front and rear edges of a pair of tires, while camber describes the wheel's inward or outward tilt as seen from directly in front of the vehicle. These are distinct angles measured in different reference planes and require separate corrections. Confusing the two on a work order or diagnosis can lead a technician to adjust the wrong component entirely.
  260. The correct answer is C (The trailer axle group, since the feathering is isolated there): because the feathered wear is confined to the trailer tandem while the tractor's own steer and drive tires wear normally, the toe problem responsible for that feathering pattern almost certainly lies in the trailer's own axle alignment rather than in the tractor. Feathering does not always originate at the steer axle, and drive axle torque transfer does not by itself create a scrubbing toe condition on a separate, unpowered trailer axle.
  261. The correct answer is B (Wear concentrated on the corresponding leaning edge of the tread): excessive camber in either direction, positive or negative, concentrates the tire's contact patch and wear toward the edge of the tread that the wheel is leaning toward. Even tread wear is the outcome of correct alignment and inflation, not incorrect camber. Saw-tooth wear and scalloped cupping are instead associated with a lack of rotation on free-rolling tires and with suspension or wheel-end oscillation problems respectively.
  262. The correct answer is B (Shims or tapered bushings at the axle mounting point): caster on a heavy truck is typically set through shims or tapered bushings installed at the spring or axle mounting, changing the angle at which the steering axis leans forward or rearward. Tie rod length changes affect toe rather than caster, and pitman arm or drag link work relates to the steering linkage's motion transfer rather than the static geometric angle of the steering axis itself.
  263. The correct answer is D (The truck would travel crabbed relative to the frame centreline): an out of tolerance thrust angle at the rear tandem causes the vehicle to dog-track, travelling crabbed relative to its actual heading, even when the steer axle's own camber and toe are perfectly within specification. Correct front geometry alone cannot compensate for a rear axle that is not tracking parallel to the frame. Feathering and single shoulder wear are symptoms tied to steer axle toe and camber problems, not to a rear thrust angle fault.
  264. The correct answer is C (The top of the tire leans outward away from the vehicle): positive camber means the top of the tire tilts outward, away from the centreline of the vehicle, when viewed from the front. This is distinct from toe out, which describes a front to rear spacing difference across an axle rather than a vertical tilt of an individual wheel, and from caster, which describes the steering axis lean viewed from the side rather than the wheel's own tilt from the front.
  265. The correct answer is B (Measure the axle beam directly for bend using specification tools): when camber cannot be brought to specification through normal adjustment and repeatedly drifts back out, the axle beam itself should be measured for a bend using appropriate axle checking equipment, since a bent beam changes the wheel's mounting angle in a way that shims cannot correct. Air spring pressure and height control valve settings affect ride height, not the physical geometry of the axle beam, and a tie rod replacement addresses toe, not camber.
  266. The correct answer is B (Feathering caused by sideways scrubbing of the tread): because an incorrect toe setting causes the tire to scrub sideways with every rotation even during straight line travel, toe is the angle most directly linked to feathered tread wear. Cupping is instead linked to suspension and wheel-end oscillation problems, while centre wear and both-shoulder wear are linked to inflation pressure rather than to the toe angle itself.
  267. The correct answer is B (One truck has toe in and the other has toe out): the direction of the feathered edge, whether the sharp edge lands on the inner or outer side of the rib, corresponds to whether the axle is set with toe in or toe out, since the scrubbing direction reverses between the two conditions. Caster and camber errors do not reverse a feather direction in this way, and a factory tire defect would not explain a wear pattern appearing consistently after an alignment procedure on both vehicles.
  268. The correct answer is A (The centreline of the frame, running front to rear): thrust angle is measured by comparing the direction the rear axle centreline actually points against the true centreline of the frame running front to rear, and a mismatch between the two produces the dog-tracking behaviour described in this section. Drag link and pitman arm angles relate to steer axle linkage motion, and drive shaft angle relates to driveline vibration concerns rather than to the geometric tracking of the axle relative to the frame.
  269. The correct answer is B (The weight and mileage these vehicles accumulate magnify small errors): although heavy truck alignment uses the same fundamental angles as a car, the far greater axle loads and annual mileage these vehicles accumulate magnify the consequences of even a small alignment error, accelerating tire wear and increasing the cost of getting it wrong. Heavy trucks use recirculating ball steering gears rather than rack and pinion, and they still rely on positive caster for self centering, so both of those statements are inaccurate.
  270. The correct answer is C (Rotating the rear axle changed the vehicle's centreline reference used for toe): because toe is measured relative to the vehicle's thrust line rather than a fixed physical mark, correcting a rear axle's thrust angle changes the reference the front toe measurement is compared against, meaning steer axle toe should always be rechecked and, if needed, adjusted after any thrust angle correction. This is a real geometric relationship between the two angles, not a rack calibration issue or an unrelated coincidence, and wheelbase itself is unaffected by an offset bushing correction of this kind.
  271. The correct answer is D (Excessive positive caster, which noticeably increases required steering effort): caster is the forward or rearward tilt of the steering axis viewed from the side, and excessive positive caster, where the top of the steering axis leans rearward, increases steering effort even though it also improves straight line stability and self centering. Camber and toe are measured from the front rather than the side of the vehicle, and thrust angle describes rear axle tracking rather than the steering axis tilt at the front.
  272. The correct answer is D (A vague, unstable feel and poor self centering after turns): low caster on both sides reduces the truck's self centering tendency, producing the vague, wandering feel and reluctance to return to centre after a turn described in this section, especially at highway speed. A one sided brake pull would instead point to a mechanical brake imbalance, steering wheel vibration typically points to a wheel-end or driveline issue, and a grinding noise inside the gear housing points to internal wear rather than a caster angle measurement.
  273. The correct answer is C (Caster is viewed from the side, camber is viewed from the front): caster describes the steering axis tilt when the truck is viewed from the side, while camber describes the wheel's inward or outward lean when viewed from the front of the vehicle. Toe and thrust angle are both essentially measured in a plan, or overhead, sense comparing distances or headings across the axle, so pairing toe with a side view or thrust angle with a front view mismatches the correct reference plane.
  274. The correct answer is B (The technician will have unknowingly set toe against a skewed reference): because toe is properly set relative to the vehicle's actual thrust line rather than an assumed straight centreline, skipping the thrust angle check means the steer axle toe may be adjusted to align with a rear axle that is itself skewed, leaving the truck still dog-tracking despite a technically correct looking steer axle alignment. The truck would not drive straight in this case, cupping is a suspension oscillation symptom unrelated to this oversight, and fuel economy would not improve under a persistent thrust angle fault.
  275. The correct answer is D (The three primary alignment angles checked on a steer axle): camber, caster, and toe are described as the three primary alignment angles checked on a heavy truck steer axle, since together they determine tire wear, steering effort, and directional stability. The Ackermann relationship instead describes how the two steer knuckles turn in proportion to each other during a turn, while wheel-end bearing preload and suspension deflection are separate mechanical measurements unrelated to these three geometric angles.
  276. The correct answer is A (A load dependent change in geometry from a worn or damaged component): a pull that only appears once the vehicle is loaded, even though static toe measured correctly at rest, points toward a worn bushing, a damaged spring, or another component that allows the alignment geometry to shift under load rather than a simple static toe error. Dismissing the complaint or assuming the static measurement was wrong ignores this load dependent behaviour, which is a recognized diagnostic pattern worth investigating further under a simulated or actual load.
  277. The correct answer is D (Radial body ply cords run straight across from bead to bead): in a radial tire, the body ply cords run radially, straight from bead to bead, with a separate steel belt package laid at an angle underneath the tread to stabilize it. A bias-ply tire instead uses body plies that crisscross at an angle to each other rather than running straight, which is the reverse of what one of the incorrect options describes, and radial construction still includes a defined sidewall separate from the tread area.
  278. The correct answer is B (Running cooler, lasting longer, and improving fuel economy): radial tires became the highway standard because they run cooler, provide longer tread life, and deliver better fuel economy than the older bias-ply design, all of which matter significantly over the high annual mileage a commercial fleet accumulates. Radial tires still require regular pressure checks, purchase cost is not the primary driver of the industry shift, and load rating is set by the load range designation on the sidewall rather than by the ply construction type alone.
  279. The correct answer is D (The load range marking on the tire sidewall): the load range indicates a tire's maximum load capacity along with its corresponding maximum inflation pressure, and a technician reads this marking to confirm the tire is correctly rated for the axle position and load it will carry. The DOT number instead identifies the manufacturing plant and date, the size designation describes the tire's physical dimensions, and the brand and tread pattern name carry no load or pressure rating information at all.
  280. The correct answer is A (The week and year the tire was manufactured): the final four digits of the DOT identification number give the week and year of manufacture, letting a technician identify a tire that has aged out of service even if its tread still appears serviceable, since rubber compounds degrade over time regardless of use. Maximum pressure and load range are separate sidewall markings, and factory original tread depth is not encoded in the DOT number at all.
  281. The correct answer is A (The tire's rubber compound has aged past a safe service life): because rubber compounds degrade with age regardless of how much use or tread wear has actually occurred, a tire identified through its DOT date code as too old can be a safety concern even with substantial legal tread depth remaining. Remaining tread depth is still a valid and important safety measurement generally, but it does not override the separate risk introduced by age related rubber degradation, and this scenario has nothing to do with an illegible marking or an incorrect size.
  282. The correct answer is D (Cupping, caused by a suspension or wheel-end oscillation problem): cupping describes evenly spaced, scalloped dips around a tire's circumference and results from something allowing the tire to bounce or oscillate repeatedly, such as a worn shock absorber, a loose wheel bearing, an out of balance tire, or an out of round brake drum. Feathering instead produces a sharp versus rounded edge along the tread ribs, centre wear is a broad zone limited to the middle of the tread, and saw-tooth wear develops diagonally across tread blocks on unrotated tires.
  283. The correct answer is B (An incorrect toe setting scrubbing the tread sideways): incorrect toe produces a feathered tread wear pattern rather than the scalloped, evenly spaced cupping described in this scenario, so it is not one of the typical causes of cupping. A worn shock absorber, a loose wheel bearing, an out of balance tire, and an out of round brake drum are all recognized causes of the oscillation that produces cupping and its accompanying vibration, making them each a reasonable first line of diagnosis in this situation.
  284. The correct answer is C (The brake drum for out of round condition): with the shock absorber, wheel bearing end play, and tire balance all confirmed acceptable, an out of round brake drum remains one of the recognized causes of cupping and the associated vibration, and checking drum runout is the logical next diagnostic step. Steer axle toe and height control valve settings would not produce this specific oscillation pattern on a drive axle tire, and the tire's load range marking has no relationship to a cupping wear pattern at all.
  285. The correct answer is B (The tire has been run consistently overinflated for an extended period): wear concentrated in the centre of the tread with the shoulders relatively unworn indicates chronic overinflation, since the tire's contact patch bulges outward at the centre under excess pressure and rides primarily on that portion of the tread. Underinflation instead produces the opposite pattern, wearing both shoulders while leaving the centre relatively unworn, and camber and toe problems produce shoulder or feathered wear rather than a centre concentrated pattern.
  286. The correct answer is D (Underinflation, with a risk of excess heat and highway tire failure): wear concentrated on both shoulders with the centre relatively unworn indicates chronic underinflation, which generates excess internal heat and is described as a leading cause of tire failure at highway speed, making this an urgent safety flag rather than a minor cosmetic wear note. Overinflation instead produces centre wear, and camber or caster problems produce single shoulder wear or handling symptoms rather than this specific both-shoulder pattern.

Practice Test 6 Answer Key

  1. The correct answer is A (Trailer tires, linked to a lack of periodic rotation): diagonal or saw-tooth wear across the tread blocks is particularly common on trailer tires and is often linked to a lack of rotation combined with the natural tendency of a free-rolling, non-driven tire to develop this pattern over a long service life. Steer tire wear patterns are more commonly linked to camber, caster, or toe issues rather than this specific rotation related saw-tooth pattern, and drive tire torque is not identified as the cause of this particular wear type.
  2. The correct answer is C (Implementing a scheduled periodic tire rotation program): since saw-tooth wear on trailer tires is linked to a lack of rotation combined with the free-rolling tire's natural tendency to develop this pattern, a scheduled rotation program directly addresses the root cause. Overinflating a tire beyond its rated maximum pressure is unsafe and unrelated to this wear pattern, trailer axles typically do not have an adjustable caster angle in the way a steer axle does, and switching tire construction types does not correct an existing rotation practice issue.
  3. The correct answer is C (It identifies the tire's physical dimensions for fitment): the size designation on a tire sidewall describes its physical dimensions, information a technician needs to confirm correct fitment for the axle and wheel being serviced. Date of manufacture is instead found in the DOT identification number, alignment specifications come from the vehicle manufacturer's own service data rather than the tire itself, and rotation intervals are set by fleet maintenance schedules rather than by a sidewall marking on the tire.
  4. The correct answer is C (The radial tire's lower operating temperature and longer expected tread life): radial construction runs cooler and provides longer tread life along with improved fuel economy, all of which make it the preferred choice for highway drive axle service over a bias-ply alternative in otherwise equal condition. Radial tires do not use a crisscrossed body ply, that description applies to bias-ply construction, and both tire types are checked using a standard tire pressure gauge, so that final option misstates a real limitation.
  5. The correct answer is B (To stabilize the tread area beneath the belt package): the steel belt package laid at an angle beneath the tread in a radial tire exists to stabilize that portion of the tire, which is part of why radial construction runs cooler and lasts longer than the older bias-ply design. The DOT information and load rating are printed on the sidewall rather than carried by the belt package, and sealing against the rim's bead seat is a function of the tire's bead area, not the tread's internal belt structure.
  6. The correct answer is D (Both shoulders worn heavily from prolonged chronic underinflation): because chronic underinflation generates excess internal heat and is identified as a leading cause of tire failure at highway speed, heavy both-shoulder wear from this cause represents the most urgent safety concern of the four patterns listed. A mild feather, a slightly faster wearing shoulder, and a light saw-tooth pattern are all worth correcting but do not carry the same immediate risk of a sudden, heat related tire failure at speed.
  7. The correct answer is A (Whether the tire's maximum load capacity is adequate for that axle position): the load range marking confirms a tire's maximum load capacity and its corresponding maximum inflation pressure, allowing a technician to verify the tire is rated adequately for the axle position and expected load it will carry. Tread pattern approval, manufacture date, and winter compound softness are each addressed by other information or by the technician's own judgment rather than by the load range marking itself.
  8. The correct answer is D (The body plies crisscross at an angle relative to each other): bias-ply construction is defined by body plies that crisscross at an angle to one another, which is the opposite of the straight, bead to bead arrangement used in radial construction. Bias-ply tires still use body plies rather than eliminating them in favour of a steel belt structure, and describing the plies as running parallel to the rotational axis does not accurately capture the crisscrossed angled arrangement that defines this older construction style.
  9. The correct answer is A (Trailer tires roll freely with no driving torque applied to them): the free-rolling nature of a non-driven trailer tire, with no driving torque applied, is specifically identified as contributing to the natural tendency toward saw-tooth wear when rotation is neglected, distinguishing it from a drive tire that experiences torque during normal operation. There is no described difference in belt construction between trailer and drive tires, no stated difference in tread life expectations by position, and trailer axle alignment precision is not identified as the explanation for this wear pattern.
  10. The correct answer is A (The final four digits of the DOT identification number): the last four digits of the DOT identification number encode the week and year of manufacture, giving a technician the information needed to identify a tire that has aged out of service even with usable tread remaining, since rubber compounds degrade with age regardless of use. The tread pattern name, size designation, and brand logo location do not provide any manufacturing date information relevant to this age based safety check.
  11. The correct answer is B (Feathering points to toe, cupping points to suspension oscillation, even wear points to correct setup): feathering is tied specifically to an incorrect toe setting, cupping is tied to a suspension or wheel-end oscillation source such as a worn shock or loose bearing, and even wear across the full tread indicates the axle's alignment and inflation are both within an acceptable range. The other three pairings mismatch these wear patterns against causes not actually associated with them in this diagnostic framework.
  12. The correct answer is C (The tread centre only, caused by chronic overinflation): centre concentrated tread wear, with the shoulders comparatively unworn, is the result of chronic overinflation, since excess pressure bulges the tire's contact patch outward toward the centre of the tread. Underinflation instead produces the opposite pattern, wearing both shoulders while leaving the centre relatively unworn, so pairing centre wear with underinflation or shoulder wear with overinflation reverses the actual relationship described in this section.
  13. The correct answer is A (The overinflated condition directly produced the observed centre wear): a documented history of sustained overinflation followed by heavy centre wear on the same tire is consistent with the established cause and effect relationship, since excess pressure bulges the contact patch toward the centre of the tread and accelerates wear there specifically. Both-shoulder wear is instead associated with underinflation, the opposite condition, and centre wear is specifically an inflation related pattern rather than one caused by an alignment angle error.
  14. The correct answer is C (Whether wear is concentrated at both shoulders or only in the centre): underinflation and overinflation are distinguished visually by the location of the wear, both shoulders for underinflation versus only the centre for overinflation, making this the correct diagnostic focus. A sharp versus rounded rib edge instead identifies a toe problem through feathering, a scalloped evenly spaced pattern identifies cupping from suspension oscillation, and the DOT date code addresses tire age rather than inflation related wear.
  15. The correct answer is D (Size designation, load range, and DOT identification number): a tire sidewall is described as carrying its size designation, its load range, and its DOT identification number, giving a technician fitment, load and pressure rating, and manufacturing date information all from the same component. Alignment angles, wheel-end bearing information, and air ride component details are all separate systems entirely and are not printed on a tire's sidewall at all.
  16. The correct answer is C (Rubber compounds degrade with age regardless of how much tread remains): the correct reasoning is that a tire's rubber compound degrades over time regardless of usage, so a tire identified as too old through its DOT date code can be unsafe even with substantial legal tread remaining. This has nothing to do with a measurement error or a worn off load range marking, and tread depth remains an important and valid measurement generally, it simply is not the only consideration when a tire's age is also a factor.
  17. The correct answer is A (Radial tires run cooler than bias-ply tires in comparable service): radial construction is specifically described as running cooler than the older bias-ply design, contributing to its longer service life and improved fuel economy in highway commercial use. It is not accurate to say radial tires run hotter, that the two constructions run at essentially the same temperature, or that the crisscrossed bias-ply structure produces a cooler running tire, since the described relationship runs the opposite direction.
  18. The correct answer is D (The wheel bearing end play and overall tire and wheel balance): because a worn shock absorber is only one of several recognized causes of cupping, alongside a loose wheel bearing, an out of balance tire, and an out of round brake drum, a technician whose shock replacement did not resolve the complaint should systematically check these remaining causes next. Toe misalignment produces feathering rather than cupping, and neither a tire's age nor its size designation is identified as a cause of this specific oscillation related wear pattern.
  19. The correct answer is A (Because installing an undersized load range tire risks overload and failure): confirming that a tire's load range and pressure rating meet or exceed the axle position's requirement matters because installing a tire with an inadequate load range risks overloading the tire under normal operating weight, increasing the risk of a heat related failure. The DOT number remains valid regardless of installation position, mixed radial and bias-ply pairing concerns relate to specific axle groupings rather than a blanket legal prohibition everywhere, and tread pattern and load range are two separate, unrelated pieces of sidewall information.
  20. The correct answer is D (Feathering, detected by running a bare hand across the tread): a technician can often diagnose incorrect toe simply by running a bare hand across the tread and feeling for the sharp versus smooth transition that defines feathering, without needing an alignment rack at all. Cupping and centre wear are typically identified through visual inspection rather than ride height observation or tread depth measurement alone, and saw-tooth wear is a visual and tactile pattern rather than something diagnosed primarily by listening for road noise.
  21. The correct answer is A (An out of balance tire and wheel assembly): an out of balance tire and wheel assembly is listed among the recognized causes of cupping, alongside a worn shock absorber, a loose wheel bearing, and an out of round brake drum, since each allows the tire to oscillate against the road surface. A loose tie rod end or a torn drag link dust boot are steering linkage defects rather than causes of cupping, and excessive toe out produces feathering, a distinctly different wear pattern from the scalloped cupping described here.
  22. The correct answer is B (Improving the accuracy and consistency of toe adjustments during alignment): since feathering is caused specifically by an incorrect toe setting scrubbing the tread sideways, improving how accurately and consistently toe is set during each alignment directly addresses the root cause without requiring additional labour hours beyond doing the existing work correctly. Switching tire construction types does not correct a toe setting error, overinflating tires above their rated maximum is unsafe and unrelated to toe, and reducing bearing inspections addresses cupping risk factors rather than feathering.
  23. The correct answer is C (The last four digits of the DOT identification number): the final four digits of the DOT identification number specifically encode the week and year a tire was manufactured, which is the exact information needed to evaluate its age against a safe service life regardless of remaining tread depth. The load range letter, tread pattern name, and size designation each carry entirely different information and do not indicate a manufacturing date at all.
  24. The correct answer is A (Feathering to toe, single shoulder wear to camber, centre wear to overinflation): feathering results from an incorrect toe setting scrubbing the tread sideways, single shoulder wear results from excessive camber tilting the wheel toward one side, and centre wear results from chronic overinflation bulging the contact patch outward at the middle of the tread. The other groupings mismatch these three wear patterns against causes that are not actually the ones described as producing them in this chapter.
  25. The correct answer is A (Because each pattern points backward to a specific mechanical cause that should also be corrected): a trained eye can look at a worn tire and work backward to identify a mechanical problem elsewhere in the vehicle, such as incorrect toe, camber, inflation, or a suspension oscillation source, and correcting that underlying cause is necessary to prevent the replacement tire from wearing the same way. Simply replacing the tire without this diagnostic step leaves the root cause unaddressed, and tire wear diagnosis is very much a tested and expected skill for this trade.
  26. The correct answer is A (It retains the hub lubricant inside while keeping outside water and dirt out): the wheel seal sits directly behind the inner bearing on the spindle and forms the barrier between the lubricated hub cavity and the outside environment. If it fails, lubricant can leak onto the brake drum or contaminants can enter and quickly wear out the bearings. Carrying vehicle weight and setting bearing clearance are separate jobs handled by the bearings themselves, not the seal.
  27. The correct answer is D (The bearing will overheat under excessive preload and fail well ahead of schedule): tapered roller bearings need a small specified amount of axial free movement, and near-zero end play applies excessive preload that generates heat inside the bearing during operation, breaking down the lubricant and wearing the rollers and races prematurely. Excessive end play, not too little, is what typically produces wobble, and preload never corrects itself with driving.
  28. The correct answer is A (The bearings, internal spacer, and seal arrive pre-adjusted as one sealed cartridge unit): a unitized or pre-set hub is built with its bearings, spacer, and seal already assembled and adjusted at the factory, so the technician installs the whole cartridge and simply torques the spindle nut to specification rather than setting end play manually. Correct spindle nut torque and a functioning wheel seal are both still required on this design.
  29. The correct answer is C (Water has worked its way past the wheel seal and contaminated the lubricant): a milky or cloudy appearance in hub oil is a classic sign of water intrusion, usually through a worn or damaged wheel seal, and it means the lubricant has already lost much of its protective ability. Metallic contamination instead gives oil a dark, gritty look rather than a milky one, and this appearance is never expected from fresh synthetic lubricant.
  30. The correct answer is B (A worn or loose wheel bearing letting the tire bounce or oscillate as it rolls): cupping, the evenly spaced scalloped dip pattern, points toward something allowing the tire to oscillate as it rotates, and a worn shock, loose bearing, or out of round drum are the classic remaining causes once alignment has already been confirmed correct. Under or overinflation instead produce shoulder or centre-focused tread wear, and a missed toe reading is ruled out here since alignment already checked within specification.
  31. The correct answer is D (It sets the retaining clamping load that keeps the pre-adjusted cartridge properly seated): even though a unitized hub arrives pre-adjusted internally, the spindle nut still supplies the clamping force that holds the entire cartridge firmly seated and secured on the spindle, and getting this torque wrong can allow the assembly to shift or loosen over time. Spindle nut torque has no bearing on hub cap fit and does not reposition an already fixed wheel seal.
  32. The correct answer is C (Re-torquing the wheel nuts because the mating surfaces settle as they seat under load): after any wheel removal and reinstallation, the mating surfaces between the wheel, hub, and fasteners can settle slightly as they seat together under real driving load, so wheel nuts must always be re-torqued after the first fifty to one hundred kilometres. A loose wheel is one of the most dangerous defects a commercial vehicle can carry, and neither draining lubricant nor replacing a seal is required simply because a wheel was changed.
  33. The correct answer is D (It applies clamping force evenly across the wheel so it seats squarely against the hub): tightening in a star pattern gradually and evenly draws the wheel down square against the mounting face, avoiding the uneven seating that can result from fully tightening one side before the other. Every nut must still reach full specified torque and the fastener count never changes, and this sequence has a genuine mechanical purpose rather than being just a habit.
  34. The correct answer is B (The wheel has been loose against the hub at some point during its service life): elongated stud holes develop when a wheel has worked loose and shifted slightly against the studs under load, gradually wearing the holes out of their original round shape. This is treated as a serious defect since it shows the fasteners were not properly clamping the wheel at some point, while overinflation affects tread wear and this pattern is not a manufacturing defect.
  35. The correct answer is D (Fine particulate can reflect normal gradual wear-in, while coarse bright flakes suggest active spalling): a small amount of very fine, dull wear debris can be consistent with normal gradual break-in wear over a long service life, while larger, bright, coarse metallic flakes point instead to active surface fatigue or spalling that needs prompt attention. Treating both findings identically would miss this real distinction, and fine grey particulate does not indicate water intrusion, which instead produces a milky appearance.
  36. The correct answer is D (The cup, which is pressed permanently into the bore of the wheel hub itself): the cup is the stationary outer race of a tapered roller bearing, pressed into the hub bore, while the cone is the inner race assembly including the rollers that rides on the spindle. The cage separately holds and spaces the rollers within the cone, and the spindle is the fixed axle shaft the assembly rotates around, not a bearing race at all.
  37. The correct answer is C (It allows a technician to visually check lubricant level and condition through a sight window): many oil bath hubs use a clear window in the hub cap so a technician can quickly check the oil level against the fill line and look for milky or metallic contamination without any disassembly, which suits infrequent stops on a long route. Oil bath hubs still use the same tapered roller bearing design, still depend on a working wheel seal, and are not immune to water contamination if that seal fails.
  38. The correct answer is C (It provides one lip retaining lubricant and a second lip excluding outside contaminants): a double-lip wheel seal typically uses one lip oriented to hold lubricant inside the hub and a second lip oriented to keep water, dirt, and road debris from working their way in, which is especially valuable in harsh gravel road service. This design has nothing to do with spindle nut torque, cost reduction is not the intent, and no hub is designed to run without lubricant.
  39. The correct answer is B (Heat from a dragging brake has transferred into the hub and warmed the lubricant): a dragging brake generates excessive heat at the drum, and that heat can conduct into the adjacent hub and bearing assembly, warming the lubricant even though the bearing itself may be perfectly serviceable. Excessive end play more commonly produces looseness and wobble rather than heat from a separate cause, and neither overfilled oil nor tire pressure explains a hot brake drum on that same wheel.
  40. The correct answer is D (Excessive free play present in the wheel bearing assembly on that wheel end): rocking a raised wheel at the twelve and six o'clock positions and feeling a clunk with visible in-and-out movement is a standard way to detect excess wheel bearing end play, since the bearing is what allows this specific type of vertical rocking. Steering linkage looseness is more typically checked at the three and nine o'clock positions instead, and neither underinflation nor an air bag issue produces a clunk felt directly at the hub.
  41. The correct answer is A (It carries the correct NLGI consistency grade and is rated for wheel bearing temperatures): wheel bearing grease must meet an appropriate National Lubricating Grease Institute grade and be formulated to withstand the heat generated inside a rotating wheel end, since an unsuitable grease can break down under heat and fail to protect the bearing. Cost, colour matching, and a recent manufacture date are not valid criteria for choosing wheel bearing lubricant.
  42. The correct answer is B (It seats the bearing rollers and races fully before the final light adjustment is made): torquing the spindle nut to a specified value and then backing it off seats the tapered rollers firmly against their races, removing any assembly slack, before the nut is brought back to a lighter final torque to set correct end play. This step has nothing to do with lubricant level, seal orientation, or wheel stud torque, which are separate and unrelated checks.
  43. The correct answer is C (Aluminum can respond differently to clamping load and heat cycling compared with steel): aluminum wheels can behave differently under clamping force and thermal cycling than steel wheels, so manufacturers often publish specific torque values and re-torque schedules for aluminum to keep the wheel properly seated over time. Aluminum wheels still require a specific torque value and still need re-torquing, and switching wheel material does not by itself change the bolt circle pattern.
  44. The correct answer is B (Lubricant can seep past the cap while air or moisture enters the cavity): the hub cap gasket seals the cap against the hub, and a cracked or missing gasket allows lubricant to weep out past the cap while letting air and moisture enter the cavity, both of which can degrade the lubricant over time. A damaged gasket has no direct effect on bearing end play, spindle nut torque, or wheel nut torque specification.
  45. The correct answer is C (A stable minor residue differs from an active leak that is depleting lubricant and needs repair): a small, unchanging film of residue with a lubricant level that stays correct at the fill line is generally treated as a minor weep to keep monitoring, while an active dripping leak that is visibly depleting hub oil indicates a failing seal or gasket needing prompt repair before the bearing runs dry. Treating both identically, ignoring either one, or assuming complete seal failure from a stable minor residue would all be wrong conclusions.
  46. The correct answer is C (On or integrated with the hub or bearing assembly at the wheel end): the ABS tone ring is mounted at the wheel end, typically on or built into the hub or bearing assembly, so a nearby wheel speed sensor can read its teeth as the wheel rotates and determine wheel speed for the system. It is not located in the brake chamber, the transmission, or on the steering knuckle, none of which rotate at wheel speed.
  47. The correct answer is D (On a full-float axle the hub and bearings, rather than the axle shaft, support the weight): in a full-float design the hub rides on its own bearings on a fixed spindle, and the axle shaft only transmits driving torque, so the shaft can be removed without the wheel falling off. On a semi-float axle the axle shaft itself supports vehicle weight in addition to transmitting torque, full-float axles still use wheel bearings, and semi-float axles remain common on lighter-duty applications.
  48. The correct answer is D (Press out the damaged stud and press in a correctly fitted replacement stud in its place): a broken or sheared wheel stud must be properly removed, typically pressed or driven out, and replaced with the correct new stud pressed into the hub to the proper fit, since studs are a precision press fit designed to hold clamping load. Leaving a damaged stud in place is unsafe even with a minimum count met, welding a stud onto the flange is not accepted, and every stud including the new one must still be torqued correctly.
  49. The correct answer is B (High-pressure water forced its way past a worn or damaged wheel seal into the hub): a worn or marginal wheel seal that might otherwise hold back ordinary road spray can be overwhelmed by the concentrated, high-pressure stream at a truck wash, forcing water past the lip and into the hub. Pressure washing does not directly cause bearing spalling, a properly sealed hub generally resists this exposure, and hub oil does not separate on its own without an outside contaminant.
  50. The correct answer is C (The outer bearing likely faced a more severe local condition, such as marginal preload or starvation): when one bearing in a hub shows significantly more wear than the other, the technician should look for a localized cause specific to that position, such as an out of specification preload adjustment or reduced lubricant reaching that bearing. Bearings do not necessarily wear identically, a failed seal is not confirmed by this evidence alone, and an oil level being too high is not tied specifically to only the outer position.
  51. The correct answer is A (Spalling, the fatigue pitting and flaking of material off a hardened bearing race surface): spalling refers to fatigue-related pitting or flaking of material from a bearing race or roller surface, typically caused by prolonged cyclic loading, contamination, or lubrication breakdown over time. Feathering and cupping are tire tread wear patterns rather than bearing failure modes, and toeing describes a wheel alignment angle, not a bearing condition at all.
  52. The correct answer is B (Brinelling, caused by static load or vibration while the bearing was not rotating): brinelling produces small indentations in the race spaced exactly at the roller pitch, typically resulting from a stationary bearing subjected to vibration or static load, such as during long-term shipping or storage, rather than from normal in-service rotation. It is a different mechanism than spalling, and while water contamination causes its own separate damage pattern, it does not produce this specific evenly spaced indentation.
  53. The correct answer is D (It holds and evenly spaces the individual tapered rollers around the cone assembly): the cage retains and evenly spaces the tapered rollers as they travel around the cone, preventing them from bunching together or shifting out of alignment during rotation. It does not seal lubricant, which is the wheel seal's job, and it does not carry vehicle weight or transmit torque on its own.
  54. The correct answer is D (A hub-piloted wheel centres on the hub, while a stud-piloted wheel is centred by studs): in a hub-piloted system the wheel is centred and located by a machined pilot on the hub, with the nuts mainly providing clamping force, while a stud-piloted system centres the wheel using the studs themselves along with specifically shaped nuts. Both systems require specified torque values, the nut designs differ between them, and hub-piloted wheels are common on drive and trailer axles as well as steering axles.
  55. The correct answer is A (The hub has run excessively hot at some point, likely from overheating or lubricant breakdown): bluish or straw-coloured discoloration on a bearing race combined with a burnt odour in the grease indicates the metal reached temperatures high enough to change its surface colour, typically pointing to overheating from excessive preload, lubricant loss, or lubricant breakdown. Bearing races are not painted blue for identification, this appearance is not normal cosmetic variation, and it is inconsistent with a recently and correctly serviced hub.
  56. The correct answer is B (It shows the exact reference level the hub oil should be maintained at): the fill line on a hub sight glass gives the technician or driver a clear visual reference for the correct oil level, so the hub can be quickly checked without removing the hub cap. It has no relationship to spindle nut torque, wheel seal position, or a bearing replacement interval, all of which are governed by separate specifications.
  57. The correct answer is C (An incline can make the oil appear higher or lower than its true level): because the oil surface settles according to gravity, checking the level while the vehicle sits on an incline can make the reading appear artificially high or low compared to how it would look on level ground, risking an incorrect fill decision. The fill line itself is a fixed physical mark that does not move with vehicle position, and it is not accurate to say incline has no effect at all.
  58. The correct answer is A (It could apply an inaccurate clamping force, risking either a loose wheel or damaged fasteners): a torque wrench that has drifted out of calibration can deliver a clamping force that is too low, risking a loose wheel over time, or too high, risking overstressed studs or nuts, either of which is a serious wheel-end safety concern. Torque wrenches can and do drift with use and time, this issue is not limited to aluminum wheels, and it has nothing to do with fuel efficiency.
  59. The correct answer is A (A dial indicator mounted to measure both lateral and radial runout at the rim): a dial indicator set up against the rim directly measures lateral and radial runout, helping the technician determine whether a bent rim is contributing to a vibration, as distinct from a bearing problem that would instead be checked with a shake or rock test at the hub. A torque wrench, tire pressure gauge, and tape measure are not appropriate or precise enough tools for this measurement.
  60. The correct answer is D (The seals were installed backwards, which is the likely root cause of the repeated failures): a wheel seal lip must face the lubricant it is meant to retain, and finding the same reversed orientation across multiple failed units points strongly toward an installation error as the root cause rather than coincidence or normal wear out. Seal orientation absolutely affects hub performance, and a consistent pattern across several units is evidence of a systemic cause, not random chance.
  61. The correct answer is B (This concept is generally known as the lubed-for-life bearing service concept): some unitized hub assemblies are described as lubed-for-life, meaning they are pre-lubricated and sealed at the factory with the intent of running for an extended interval without routine repacking. Full-float and semi-float describe how vehicle weight is supported at the axle, not lubrication service intervals, and star pattern torque sequencing refers to wheel nut installation rather than bearing lubrication at all.
  62. The correct answer is B (A narrow range balances avoiding excessive preload against avoiding excessive bearing looseness): the specified end play range is kept narrow because too little end play creates excessive preload that overheats the bearing, while too much end play allows the wheel to wobble and wear unevenly, so the tight tolerance keeps the bearing operating in its intended range. This tolerance is not arbitrary, it applies regardless of hub material, and it has no effect on whether a seal can physically be installed.
  63. The correct answer is A (It maintains a fixed distance between the bearings to preserve the factory-set end play): the internal spacer holds the inner and outer bearing cones at a precise, fixed distance apart so that once the spindle nut is torqued to specification, the factory pre-set end play is achieved and maintained without any further field adjustment. It plays no role in generating torque, does not eliminate the need for lubricant, and is a functional rather than decorative part.
  64.
