The correct answer is C (Remove the wheel from service since a cracked wheel is not safe to keep operating): a wheel found cracked around a stud hole or rim flange must be removed from service, since a crack can propagate under the repeated cyclic loading of highway operation and lead to sudden wheel failure. Field welding a structural wheel crack is not accepted repair practice, reducing torque does not address the structural defect, and continuing to run a cracked wheel of any severity is unsafe.
  65. The correct answer is B (It can lead to sudden wheel separation, causing loss of control or vehicle damage): a loose wheel at highway speed can progressively wear the stud holes, shear studs, and ultimately separate from the vehicle, which can cause the driver to lose control or send a detached wheel into the path of other traffic, making this an urgent safety hazard. This defect is not simply a fuel economy or comfort concern, and it requires immediate correction rather than routine monitoring.
  66. The correct answer is D (Hardened alloy steel formulated specifically for high cyclic contact loading applications): tapered roller bearing races are manufactured from hardened alloy steel specifically to resist the high contact stresses and cyclic loading present at a heavy truck wheel end over a long service life. Soft mild steel would wear and deform far too quickly under these loads, and neither cast aluminum nor plastic composite have the hardness or fatigue resistance this application requires.
  67. The correct answer is B (Pack the inner bearing and seal into the hub, slide onto spindle, install outer bearing): the correct general sequence packs and installs the inner bearing cone and the seal into the hub first, then slides the assembled hub onto the axle spindle, after which the outer bearing cone, washer, and spindle nut are installed to complete the assembly. Reversing this order or treating the sequence as unimportant risks damaging the seal or trapping components incorrectly.
  68. The correct answer is C (The contaminated friction surface will significantly reduce braking performance on that wheel): lubricant on a brake drum's friction surface reduces the coefficient of friction between the drum and shoe lining, which can severely and unpredictably reduce braking performance, making this a serious safety concern requiring cleaning or replacement of the contaminated components. Oil contamination does not improve brake performance, does not change drum diameter, and has no effect on how the bearing carries load.
  69. The correct answer is B (A dial indicator mounted to measure axial movement while pushing and pulling the hub): mounting a dial indicator against the hub and then pushing and pulling it in and out along the spindle axis gives a precise numerical reading of end play, which can be directly compared against the manufacturer's specification. Spinning the wheel by hand or checking oil level does not measure end play at all, and a tire pressure gauge has no application to this measurement.
  70. The correct answer is C (The wheel bearings, shock absorbers, and brake drums for looseness or out of round condition): once alignment is ruled out as the cause of a cupped wear pattern, the technician should turn to the wheel-end and suspension components that can allow a tire to bounce or oscillate as it rolls, specifically worn wheel bearings, worn shock absorbers, or an out of round brake drum. Tread compound, steering gear fluid, and drivetrain mounts are not the components most directly linked to producing this specific wear pattern.
  71. The correct answer is C (Its resistance to hub lubricant and heat while remaining flexible enough to seal continuously): wheel seal lips are typically made from a synthetic rubber compound engineered to resist degradation from hub lubricants and the heat generated at the wheel end, while staying flexible enough to maintain constant contact with the rotating surface it seals against. Cost reduction, skipping quality control, and sunlight resistance are not the relevant reasons this material is selected for a component sealed inside the hub.
  72. The correct answer is C (Facing toward the lubricant it is specifically designed to retain inside the hub): the primary sealing lip must face toward the lubricant cavity so hub oil or grease pressure helps maintain proper lip contact and sealing, and installing it backwards allows lubricant to leak out and contaminants to enter, leading to premature bearing failure. There is no valid orientation involving facing away from the lubricant or a ninety degree rotation, and lip direction absolutely matters.
  73. The correct answer is D (To compensate for expected settling of newly mated surfaces as the components seat under load): newly installed components, including a fresh hub assembly and wheel, can settle slightly as their mating surfaces seat together under real driving loads, so a re-torque after a short break-in interval confirms the wheel nuts remain at correct clamping force. This step is not intended to replace grease, check ABS tone ring function, or measure tread depth, all of which are unrelated maintenance items.
  74. The correct answer is D (The out of round brake drum is the more likely source of the vibration): since the wheel bearings measured within acceptable end play with no looseness detected, the out of round brake drum becomes the more likely mechanical explanation for a vibration that worsens with speed, since an out of round drum can create a cyclic disturbance during rotation. It would not be appropriate to replace bearings that tested within specification without further justification, and the drum measurement is directly relevant evidence that should not be disregarded.
  75. The correct answer is A (Dispose of it through an approved shop waste stream rather than pouring it down any drain): used wheel bearing grease, especially when contaminated with water or metal particles, must be handled as shop waste and disposed of through an approved waste stream in accordance with environmental and workplace safety practices. Pouring it down a drain, mixing it back into usable product, or storing it in an unlabeled open container are all unsafe and improper handling practices.
  76. The correct answer is A (The hub, the central component carrying the studs and supported on the spindle by the bearings): the hub is the central wheel-end component that carries the wheel studs the wheel mounts to, and it is itself supported on the axle spindle by the inner and outer bearings, allowing it to rotate freely while carrying the vehicle's weight. The kingpin, tie rod, and drag link are steering-related components and play no role in supporting the hub or its bearings.
  77. The correct answer is A (Rotate the hub by hand to confirm it spins freely without excessive drag or looseness): after torquing the spindle nut, spinning the hub by hand lets the technician confirm there is neither excessive drag, which could indicate overtightening, nor looseness or wobble, which could indicate undertightening or a misassembled cartridge. Tread depth, tire pressure, and brake chamber stroke are unrelated checks that do not confirm correct hub assembly.
  78. The correct answer is B (It reduces end play excessively, creating a high preload condition that leads to overheating): overtightening the spindle nut squeezes the bearing assembly more tightly than intended, driving end play down and creating excessive preload, which generates heat during operation and shortens bearing life rather than extending it. Overtightening reduces end play rather than increasing it, and eliminating free play entirely is harmful rather than beneficial to bearing life.
  79. The correct answer is B (Checking tire and wheel balance along with runout at each individual wheel position): a vibration that is speed dependent but does not change with braking or steering input strongly points toward a rotating imbalance or runout condition in the tires or wheels, making balance and runout checks the logical first step. Transmission fluid, parking brake cable adjustment, and washer fluid level have no realistic connection to a speed dependent vibration matching this exact description.
  80. The correct answer is D (A dial indicator set up to read axial movement of the hub against the spindle): a dial indicator mounted to detect axial, or in-and-out, movement of the hub against the fixed spindle gives the precise numerical reading needed to confirm end play falls within the narrow specified tolerance. A tape measure and tire pressure gauge are not designed for this kind of precise small movement measurement, and a visual estimate cannot reliably confirm a thousandths-of-an-inch tolerance.
  81. The correct answer is A (This part is correctly known as the axle spindle in wheel-end terminology): the axle spindle is the fixed, non-rotating shaft extending outward from the axle housing, and the hub along with its bearings is mounted on and rotates around this spindle. It is not a hydraulic brake component, a rubber seal, or a wheel fastener, all of which are entirely separate parts of the wheel-end assembly.
  82. The correct answer is C (The wheel seal positioned directly behind the inner bearing on the spindle): the wheel seal is the primary component tasked with both retaining internal lubricant and excluding outside water and dirt from the hub cavity, sitting directly behind the inner bearing where it forms a continuous rotating seal against the spindle. The hub cap gasket plays only a supporting role at the outer cap, while the wheel stud and brake drum perform entirely different functions unrelated to sealing the hub.
  83. The correct answer is A (Add the correct type and grade of oil to restore the level to the fill line): a low but clear oil reading calls for topping up the hub with the correct type and grade of lubricant to restore it to the fill line, since running a hub low on lubricant risks bearing damage even if the remaining oil has not yet become contaminated. Clear appearance does not excuse a low level, immediate full component replacement is not warranted from this finding alone, and delaying action risks the bearing running dry.
  84. The correct answer is A (This pattern is consistent with normal oxidation and heat aging of the lubricant over its interval): a gradual darkening of hub oil over an extended service period, without a milky appearance, gritty texture, or level loss, is generally consistent with ordinary oxidation and heat aging of the lubricant rather than an active failure. Milky oil would indicate water intrusion, gritty or metallic oil would suggest bearing wear, and a gradual darkening with no other symptoms does not point to a manufacturing defect.
  85. The correct answer is D (The wheel can be drawn down unevenly, risking a warped mounting surface or uneven clamping load): tightening around the wheel in a simple circle rather than a star pattern can pull the wheel down unevenly against the hub, risking a warped mounting surface or uneven clamping across the fasteners, which is exactly what the star pattern is designed to prevent. This tightening order has no direct effect on wheel bearing end play, and it does not by itself cause immediate air loss or automatic loosening.
  86. The correct answer is B (The manual field adjustment of bearing end play using feeler gauges or a dial indicator): the defining benefit of a unitized pre-set hub is that the bearings arrive already adjusted to the correct end play as a sealed cartridge, so the technician no longer needs to manually set end play using feeler gauges or a dial indicator in the field. The spindle nut torque requirement, wheel crack inspection, and tire pressure check all remain necessary steps regardless of hub design used.
  87. The correct answer is A (Remove the affected wheel from service since it is no longer considered safe to run): elongated stud holes indicate the wheel has already experienced looseness severe enough to wear the mounting holes out of round, which compromises its structural fit against the hub, so the correct response is removal from service rather than continued use anywhere on the vehicle. Simply increasing torque, shortening the inspection interval, or relocating the wheel to a different axle does not correct the underlying structural defect.
  88. The correct answer is A (Re-torquing the wheel nuts to compensate for expected settling of the mating surfaces): any time a wheel is removed and reinstalled, the mating surfaces can settle slightly as they seat under real driving load, so the wheel nuts must be re-torqued after a short follow-up mileage interval to confirm they remain at correct clamping force. Tire replacement, repainting, and rebalancing only the opposite wheel are not required simply because a wheel was removed and reinstalled.
  89. The correct answer is C (Comparing runout measured at the rim to end play and looseness measured at the hub): taking a dial indicator reading directly on the rim isolates rim-specific runout from a bent wheel, while a separate reading taken at the hub for axial movement isolates bearing-related looseness, allowing the technician to distinguish which component is actually responsible for the wobble. Tread depth, tire pressure, and grease colour do not provide the comparative runout information needed to separate these two possible causes.
  90. The correct answer is D (A wheel-end failure at highway speed with a loaded trailer can cause loss of control): wheel-end problems, including low or contaminated hub lubricant and visible leaks, can progress into bearing seizure or a loose wheel, and either outcome at highway speed with a loaded trailer is one of the most dangerous failures a commercial vehicle can experience, which is why this check is treated as safety-critical. This is not simply a paperwork exercise, and hub oil condition has a direct and serious connection to safe operation.
  91. The correct answer is C (To reduce vibration and road shock transmitted into the cab and the driver's seat): Rigid mounting would transmit every bump, pothole, and expansion joint directly into the driver, causing fatigue and potential injury over a full shift. Cab suspension isolates the driver compartment from frame flex and road irregularities instead. This improves ride comfort and reduces long term wear on the cab structure and wiring. It has no meaningful effect on aerodynamics or on how the cab is removed for major service work.
  92. The correct answer is D (Rubber isolator cushion mounts positioned at the front and rear of the cab): Bonded rubber compound sandwiched between metal plates absorbs small vibrations and some torsional twist inexpensively and simply. This design suits vocational trucks and shorter wheelbase units where cost and durability matter more than highway ride comfort. Rear air suspension paired with front pivot mounts is instead the typical long haul highway tractor arrangement. Full four corner air suspension is a higher end option, not the vocational default.
  93. The correct answer is B (Leaking air at cracks, chafing points, or connection fittings on the spring): Soapy water forms visible bubbles wherever pressurized air escapes through a defect, making otherwise hidden leaks easy to locate quickly. This is a fast, low cost diagnostic step performed before more invasive teardown inspection is attempted. Bracket torque and shock absorber condition are checked through separate physical inspection methods, not a soap test. The height control valve is checked by observing its function under load, not by spraying it with soapy water.
  94. The correct answer is A (A worn pivot bushing at the front cab mounting hinge allowing lateral movement): A worn bushing introduces play that lets the cab shift side to side, producing a clunk and stressing crossing wiring harnesses and hoses exactly as described. A properly charged air spring or a functioning shock would not by itself cause lateral shifting of this kind. Normal wear on a correctly torqued, undamaged bracket would not produce audible clunking or visible chafing marks. The combination of symptoms points directly to bushing wear as the source.
  95. The correct answer is B (Weak resistance to compression and rebound, or visible leaking fluid at the seal): A healthy shock provides firm, controlled resistance in both directions, while a dead shock allows uncontrolled bouncing and often shows leaking hydraulic fluid at the seal itself. This lack of proper damping accelerates wear on every other cab mount component over time. Firm, consistent resistance is actually the correct, healthy result and does not indicate a fault at all. Warmth after normal operation and a hiss coming from a separate air spring are unrelated to shock absorber condition.
  96. The correct answer is D (It adjusts air pressure in the rear springs to maintain consistent cab ride height): The valve monitors the distance between cab and frame and modulates spring pressure to compensate for load, settling, and temperature changes. This keeps ride quality consistent across a wide range of operating conditions throughout the day. It has nothing to do with tilt cylinder locking, trailer supply air pressure, or the ventilation system, which are entirely separate systems on the vehicle.
  97. The correct answer is C (Harsh impacts get transmitted into the frame connection points when the cab bottoms out): A cab riding too low no longer has adequate suspension travel available, so bumps compress the springs fully and transmit harsh shock loads directly into the mounting points. This accelerates wear and can eventually damage brackets over time if left unaddressed. A stuck height valve has no meaningful effect on fuel economy, tilt cab prop engagement, or trailer supply air pressure, since those are unrelated systems entirely.
  98. The correct answer is A (Virtually all cabover configurations, along with many conventional highway tractors): A cabover places the driver directly above the engine, so the entire cab must tilt forward to allow access for service work. Many conventional tractors also use tilt cab designs for exactly the same practical reason, not only cabover models. Local delivery straight trucks and vocational dump trucks are not defined primarily by this specific feature. Tilt cab design is unrelated to whether a given tractor happens to have rear air suspension for ride comfort.
  99. The correct answer is A (Shift into neutral or park, set the parking brake, and release the cab safety latch): The pre-tilt sequence requires securing the vehicle against movement and confirming that interfering components and the cab lock are clear before hydraulic pressure is ever applied. Trailer glad hands, landing gear, brake reservoirs, and fifth wheel slide pins are all unrelated to preparing a cab for tilting. Skipping the cab lock release step specifically risks bending the lock mechanism or damaging the surrounding cab structure entirely.
  100. The correct answer is C (Bending or damage occurs to the cab lock mechanism or the surrounding cab structure): Forcing hydraulic pressure against an engaged latch applies force the lock and structure were never designed to resist, risking permanent deformation of both. This is precisely why the release must always be confirmed before tilting is allowed to begin on any tractor. This action has no real connection to hydraulic fluid temperature, an automatically releasing safety prop, or trailer air pressure at the glad hands, since these are unrelated systems entirely.
  101. The correct answer is B (A safety prop, also called a safety strut or prop rod): This mechanical device physically holds the cab up regardless of hydraulic pressure, and it must be fully engaged and visually confirmed before anyone works underneath the raised cab. A height control valve, kingpin jaws, and glad hand gaskets are all unrelated components tied to cab suspension, fifth wheel coupling, and trailer air connections rather than tilt cab safety at all.
  102. The correct answer is D (A hydraulic line or seal failure could cause the cab to fall suddenly and unexpectedly): Hydraulic systems can fail without any warning at all, and if the cab is supported only by pressure, a sudden failure allows the cab to drop with catastrophic force onto anyone working underneath it. This is precisely why a mechanical prop, independent of hydraulics entirely, is treated as a non negotiable safety requirement in every shop. Fluid evaporation, insufficient lifting force, and air spring damage are not the actual reasoning behind this important safety rule.
  103. The correct answer is D (External leaks at the cylinder rod and packing gland before any other component): Correct diagnostic sequence moves from the simplest and least invasive checks toward more involved ones as needed. An external leak at the rod seal is the first and easiest thing to inspect visually before anything else. Only after ruling this out does the technician check reservoir fluid level for trapped air, then consider an internal bypass as a last resort. Jumping straight to a teardown, or checking unrelated trailer suspension components, skips this proper diagnostic sequence entirely.
  104. The correct answer is C (An internal bypass where fluid leaks past the piston seal inside the cylinder): With no external leak and correct fluid level already ruling out trapped air as the cause, fluid bypassing internally past the piston seal is the remaining explanation for gradual pressure loss. This finding calls for a cylinder rebuild or outright replacement to properly resolve the underlying issue. Trapped air was already ruled out by the confirmed correct fluid level, and a fifth wheel jaw issue would not affect tilt cab hydraulics in any way whatsoever.
  105. The correct answer is A (A low reservoir allows air to enter the system, and trapped air compresses under load): Unlike hydraulic fluid, air is compressible, so trapped air pockets allow the system to slowly settle as the air compresses under the cab's own weight, even with zero external leakage present. This represents a genuinely distinct failure mode compared to a seal leak or an internal bypass condition. It has no effect on the mechanical strength of the safety prop, the height control valve, or the cab safety latch at all.
  106. The correct answer is B (Release the prop, then slowly release hydraulic pressure to lower the cab under control): The prop is released first, and hydraulic pressure is then bled off gradually for a smooth, fully controlled descent back to the normal driving position. Releasing pressure before the prop, or releasing both at the same exact moment, removes the controlled descent this procedure is specifically designed to provide. Disconnecting the pump and letting the cab drop under gravity alone is genuinely unsafe and completely uncontrolled.
  107. The correct answer is B (A cab that looks closed but is not actually latched can shift or tilt unexpectedly): Visual appearance alone is not proof of a secure latch, and an unlatched cab poses a genuinely serious hazard if it shifts or tilts unexpectedly while the vehicle is moving down the highway. This verification applies equally to both cabover and conventional tilt cab designs, not just to one particular type of tractor. The cab lock itself has no functional connection to trailer electrical power or to cab suspension air pressure whatsoever.
  108. The correct answer is D (Disconnect or move clear any components that would interfere with or stretch during the tilt): The pre-tilt checklist specifically requires clearing any interfering hoses, ducting, and cables that could stretch or become damaged as the cab pivots forward on its hinges. Leaving everything connected risks damaging components or restricting the tilt motion partway through the procedure. Disconnecting only one type of component, or simply taping items down instead, does not actually address the real interference risk present during the tilt.
  109. The correct answer is C (The front pivots on a fixed hinge like a door, while the rear rides on air springs): This is simply the standard highway tractor design approach, using a hinge point at the front for pivoting and cushioned air springs at the rear where most cab weight and vertical movement actually occur. There is no such legal restriction on where front air springs can be placed, no inherent conflict with tilt cylinder location, and no blanket regulation mandating rubber front mounts on every single tractor built.
  110. The correct answer is A (Dampers that control lateral sway and pitching during hard braking or acceleration): A full four corner system with dampers manages roll and pitch across all mounting points, improving stability during aggressive maneuvers beyond what a rear only air spring can provide alone. This design does not eliminate all movement whatsoever, since some controlled isolation is actually the entire point of the system. It has no connection to tilt cab prop function or trailer landing gear operation at all.
  111. The correct answer is A (Wear or looseness that lets the cab shift side to side and stress crossing wiring): Bracket and bushing inspection specifically targets the mechanical play that develops as these components wear over time, since this play creates a clunk and puts real strain on hoses and harnesses crossing between the cab and frame. Air pressure in the springs, trailer connector corrosion, and fifth wheel lubrication are each checked through entirely separate inspection procedures unrelated to bracket and bushing condition.
  112. The correct answer is D (Internal pump wear or a partially restricted flow reducing pumping efficiency): A healthy pump moves the cab to full height in a fairly predictable number of strokes, so a significant increase suggests internal wear, a partial blockage, or declining pump efficiency delivering less fluid per stroke than before. A properly engaged safety prop only holds the cab up after tilting is already complete, so it does not affect stroke count at all. This performance drop is not normal, and a failed cab lock would prevent the tilt from starting entirely, not just slow it down gradually.
  113. The correct answer is B (A hydraulic pump, either hand operated or electric, and one or more tilt cylinders): These two components generate and apply the force needed to raise the cab on its hinges during any tilt operation. A leveling valve and leaf springs instead relate to suspension, not to tilting. A kingpin and locking jaws belong to fifth wheel coupling, and a seven pin connector with glad hands belongs to trailer electrical and air connections, none of which are part of the tilt mechanism itself.
  114. The correct answer is C (To ensure the prop is fully seated before anyone works underneath the raised cab): A prop that appears engaged but is not actually fully seated provides no real protection against a sudden hydraulic failure, so a deliberate visual check closes this gap before any work begins underneath. This confirmation has nothing to do with the pump handle, the trailer landing gear, or the electrical connector, all of which are unrelated to tilt cab safety verification entirely.
  115. The correct answer is C (The prop should always be engaged, since a slow sink today can become a sudden failure): A slow, gradual sink still indicates an underlying hydraulic problem, and that exact same fault can progress to a sudden, catastrophic failure with no additional warning whatsoever. The prop requirement is treated as non negotiable regardless of the job's duration or the technician's perceived reaction time. Relying on quick reflexes or job length as a substitute for a mechanical prop ignores the entire reason this important safety rule exists in the first place.
  116. The correct answer is B (Rubber isolator mounts, sometimes called cushion mounts): This bonded rubber and metal plate design is the simplest, most affordable form of cab isolation currently available, and it is common on vocational trucks and shorter wheelbase units. Air spring bellows and hydraulic shock cartridges are different components entirely, used in more advanced suspension arrangements. Transverse torsion bars are not actually a design used for heavy truck cab mounting in this trade at all.
  117. The correct answer is D (Shift into neutral or park and set the parking brake as required by the checklist): Securing the vehicle against unintended movement is a mandatory early step within the pre-tilt checklist, performed before releasing the cab lock or applying any hydraulic pressure at all. Proceeding to the safety latch instead, holding a brake pedal manually, or assuming a level floor makes this step unnecessary all bypass a genuinely required safety step with no valid justification whatsoever.
  118. The correct answer is A (Serious injuries and fatalities have resulted from improper tilt cab procedures in this trade): This is precisely why the pre-tilt checklist, the mandatory safety prop, and the required visual confirmation steps all exist in the first place, since skipping them can lead to catastrophic and permanent consequences. Cosmetic paint damage, temporary climate control loss, and minor fuel economy effects are all trivial issues, not the actual documented safety concern behind these mandatory procedures.
  119. The correct answer is D (Whether the cab safety latch has actually been released before the pump was operated): An engaged latch will prevent the cab from rising at all, even with a fully functional pump doing its job correctly, so confirming the latch release status is the logical first check before assuming a hydraulic fault exists. Trailer suspension, fifth wheel clearance, and glad hand gaskets are entirely unrelated systems and would have no effect whatsoever on whether the cab itself is physically able to tilt.
  120. The correct answer is A (The prop protects against sudden failure of any hydraulic component at any time): Even reliable hydraulic components can fail unexpectedly from a line rupture, a seal failure, or a defective fitting, and the mechanical prop provides a genuine backup that does not depend on hydraulic integrity in any way. No manufacturer actually guarantees hydraulic components will never fail, and the prop is a real functional safety device, not merely cosmetic, so removing it would clearly increase risk to technicians working underneath the cab.
  121. The correct answer is C (Some torsional twist as the frame flexes over rough or uneven terrain): Rubber isolator mounts absorb both vertical vibration and a genuine degree of torsional twisting as the frame rails flex independently over uneven road surfaces at highway speeds. Trailer lateral drift in crosswinds, sheet metal thermal expansion, and fifth wheel rotation during coupling are all unrelated phenomena that cab suspension mounts are simply not designed to address at all.
  122. The correct answer is B (A leveling valve that has stuck or failed to properly regulate air spring pressure): The leveling valve is directly responsible for maintaining correct ride height by adjusting spring air pressure as conditions change, so a stuck valve is the direct and logical cause of a persistently incorrect height reading. A safety prop, a worn kingpin, and a cracked upper coupler plate belong to tilt cab safety and trailer coupling systems, entirely unrelated to cab suspension ride height in any way.
  123. The correct answer is A (The cab may bottom out over bumps, transmitting harsh impacts into the frame connection points): Insufficient ride height reduces the available suspension travel, so the cab strikes its physical limits over bumps and transmits shock directly into the mounting hardware rather than absorbing it properly. Trailer spring brake application, ABS power loss, and fifth wheel jaw release are all unrelated outcomes tied to entirely different systems on the combination vehicle as a whole.
  124. The correct answer is B (Heavy truck frames flex significantly more under load, requiring isolation to protect the driver): Heavy truck frames experience substantially more flex and load variation than a passenger car body ever does, so isolating the cab protects the driver from the resulting vibration and shock encountered daily. There is no such legal prohibition preventing passenger cars from using isolation, truck cabs are not actually lighter than car bodies, and rigid mounting would not meaningfully improve fuel economy while significantly worsening driver comfort and fatigue over time.
  125. The correct answer is C (The mounting brackets and pivot bushings for uneven wear or looseness on one side): With the air springs already confirmed sound and holding pressure correctly, uneven side to side wear at a bracket or bushing is the logical next suspect, since asymmetric wear there produces exactly this kind of uneven ride complaint. Trailer electrical connections, fifth wheel lubrication, and landing gear gearbox condition are all unrelated to a genuine cab suspension leveling complaint of this specific type.
  126. The correct answer is D (Controlling the rate of compression and rebound to prevent excessive cab bouncing): Shocks dampen the motion of the air springs, ensuring the cab settles smoothly rather than bouncing repeatedly after absorbing a bump on the highway. Storing compressed air for spring brakes, locking tilt cylinders, and sealing trailer brake line connections are all functions of entirely different systems on the vehicle, unrelated to cab suspension damping in any meaningful way.
  127. The correct answer is B (No visible external leak at the rod seal and the fluid reservoir confirmed at correct level): Once external leakage and a low fluid level, which allows air to enter the system, have both been ruled out, an internal bypass past the piston seal remains the logical explanation for continued sinking. A visible external puddle would instead point to an external leak, a low reservoir points to trapped air, and a bent safety prop is an unrelated mechanical issue with the prop itself.
  128. The correct answer is A (The cab safety latch, sometimes called the hood latch or cab lock): This latch secures the cab firmly in its normal driving position and must be released before any hydraulic tilt pressure is ever applied. The trailer release handle for fifth wheel jaws, the landing gear crank handle, and the glad hand release lever are entirely separate components tied to trailer coupling and air connections, not to cab tilting at all.
  129. The correct answer is D (The sinking symptom can also result from external leaks, trapped air, or an internal bypass): A slow sink has several possible root causes beyond pump wear alone, so a proper diagnostic sequence rules out simpler, cheaper causes before ever considering a full pump replacement. Pumps genuinely do wear out over time, hydraulic pumps are truly part of most tilt systems, and pump wear is unrelated to how fast the cab actually sinks, so this reasoning does not support skipping proper diagnosis.
  130. The correct answer is C (Reposition the cab slightly and re-engage the prop until it is confirmed fully seated): A prop that is not fully seated cannot actually be trusted to provide reliable mechanical support in an emergency, so the correct response is to adjust and re-engage it until proper seating is visually confirmed. Proceeding with a partial seat, relying on hydraulics instead, or having a person physically hold the cab all leave the technician exposed to exactly the catastrophic failure this procedure exists to prevent.
  131. The correct answer is D (Rubber mounts offer limited isolation, while rear air suspension provides greater ride comfort): Rubber isolators are simple and inexpensive but limited in how much vibration they can absorb, while an air suspension system offers superior isolation designed specifically for long haul comfort. Rubber mounts actually require no compressed air at all, unlike air springs, and neither design is exclusive to cabover or conventional configurations specifically. Rubber mounts are also generally cheaper to produce overall, not more expensive than a full air system.
  132. The correct answer is C (Securely mounted with no missing or broken bolts, and no evidence of shifting on its mounts): Inspection criteria require completely intact mounting hardware and no detectable shifting at all in order to pass cleanly during a formal inspection. A missing bolt, visible shifting on the mounts, or a safety prop that fails to seat properly are each defects that would be flagged during inspection, not conditions that indicate a genuinely clean pass result.
  133. The correct answer is B (That the tilt mechanism and safety prop function properly and the cab locks securely): These are the specific cab related inspection points described for tilt cab systems, verifying that the mechanism works correctly and the cab secures safely for continued travel. Kingpin to jaw clearance, trailer landing gear, and glad hand gasket condition are each checked under separate categories covering the fifth wheel, trailer landing gear, and trailer air connections respectively, not the cab itself.
  134. The correct answer is A (Air has entered the hydraulic system, reducing pumping efficiency and aerating the fluid): Foamy fluid combined with reduced pumping efficiency is a classic sign of air contamination within a hydraulic circuit, since air compresses and churns rather than transmitting force efficiently through the system. A seized prop or a fully engaged latch would typically prevent tilting entirely rather than simply requiring more effort to raise. Cab air suspension pressure loss is unrelated to the tilt cylinder's separate hydraulic fluid condition.
  135. The correct answer is B (Once the cab reaches full tilt height, before any technician moves underneath it): The prop can only physically engage once the cab has actually reached the raised position, and it must be confirmed seated before anyone moves underneath it to begin working. Engaging it before tilting begins is not physically possible at all, waiting until after the repair defeats its entire safety purpose, and it has no connection to when the parking brake happens to be set.
  136. The correct answer is C (The air springs mounted at the rear of the cab where it meets the frame): These springs are specifically inspected for cracks, bulges, chafing, and leaks using both careful visual inspection and a simple soapy water test at the shop. The seven pin connector and trailer ABS unit, the kingpin and upper coupler plate, and the landing gear components are each part of separate trailer systems, not the cab suspension itself at all.
  137. The correct answer is D (Hold the tractor out of tilt related service work until the bent prop bracket is repaired): Since the mechanical prop is treated as a non negotiable safety requirement for anyone working under a raised cab, a bent bracket that prevents proper engagement must be repaired before the tilt function can safely be used again. Relying on hydraulics alone, welding the prop into a compromised position, or simply changing who performs the work underneath do not address the actual underlying safety defect present.
  138. The correct answer is A (Observe ride height consistency and re-check for leaks after the vehicle sits for a period): Watching for a change in ride height over a period of time, combined with a follow up leak recheck, confirms whether the springs are actually holding pressure rather than slowly bleeding down unnoticed. Kingpin clearance, the trailer ABS lamp circuit, and landing gear gearbox operation are all unrelated checks tied to entirely different vehicle systems, not to cab air spring pressure retention specifically.
  139. The correct answer is D (The front pivots on a fixed hinge point, similar to a door hinge, ahead of the cab): This hinge allows the cab to both pivot for tilting and flex slightly during normal driving conditions, while the rear air springs handle most of the vertical isolation work. The front does not use its own dedicated air spring matching the rear pair, is not bolted rigidly like a car body would be, and the hydraulic tilt cylinder is a separate component entirely from the structural hinge itself.
  140. The correct answer is B (A mechanical prop does not share any failure mode with the hydraulic system it backs up): A second hydraulic circuit could still fail from the same underlying causes, such as contaminated fluid or a shared reservoir problem, while a purely mechanical prop provides genuinely independent support unaffected by any hydraulic failure. There is no such regulation banning hydraulic backup circuits outright, and hydraulic fluid availability in a shop is not the actual reasoning behind choosing a mechanical prop design in the first place.
  141. The correct answer is B (Excessive clearance lets the kingpin move slightly inside worn jaws, producing the clunk and raising): Worn jaws and a worn kingpin throat create measurable play that allows small movement under load, producing the clunk the driver reported. This same play increases the risk that the jaws will not fully secure a kingpin that is itself already showing wear. Manufacturers publish a maximum allowable clearance specifically so a technician can objectively decide whether the assembly is still safe or needs repair. Neither the electrical connector, steering alignment, nor the landing gear gearbox is affected by fifth wheel jaw and kingpin wear.
  142. The correct answer is C (Document the measurement as a confirmed defect and remove the fifth wheel from service until it is repaired): An objective measurement that exceeds the published maximum is treated as a confirmed defect requiring the fifth wheel to be taken out of service until it is repaired or the worn components are replaced. Adding grease may reduce friction on the plate surface but does nothing to correct worn jaws or a worn kingpin throat, so it does not resolve the underlying defect. Waiting for a driver complaint ignores an already documented, objective safety measurement. Tire pressure on the drive axle has no relationship to fifth wheel jaw clearance whatsoever.
  143. The correct answer is B (It reduces friction so the trailer's upper coupler can pivot smoothly against the plate during turning): The top plate must stay lubricated so the trailer's upper coupler can pivot smoothly against it as the combination vehicle turns corners. A dry plate causes excessive wear on both the fifth wheel plate itself and the trailer's upper coupler surface, and can also produce hard, jerky steering as the trailer resists pivoting freely. Glad hand gaskets, the release handle linkage, and the landing gear gearbox are each separate mechanical systems that this specific lubrication task does not address at all. Visual cleanliness of the plate does not indicate whether adequate lubricant film remains between the two mating surfaces.
  144. The correct answer is A (A tug test, pulling forward gently against the set trailer brakes to confirm the coupling): An audible click alone does not guarantee that the locking jaws have actually closed completely around the kingpin shank, a condition known in the trade as a false coupling. The mandatory tug test has the driver pull forward gently against the set trailer brakes to physically confirm the connection has genuinely locked before the landing gear is raised and the trailer is no longer separately supported. Checking only the electrical connector, measuring suspension ride height, or checking tire tread depth does none of the work needed to confirm the actual mechanical coupling.
  145. The correct answer is A (A false coupling, where the jaws appear closed but never actually locked around the kingpin): A false coupling occurs when the trailer settles onto the fifth wheel's top plate and the driver believes engagement has occurred, sometimes even hearing a sound resembling the normal click, while the jaws have not actually closed securely around the kingpin. This is precisely why the mandatory tug test against the set trailer brakes exists, since it physically verifies the lock rather than relying on sound or appearance alone. A dry coupling is not a standard trade term, a slide lock failure describes a different fifth wheel slide rail problem, and reversed polarity is an electrical wiring issue unrelated to mechanical coupling.
  146. The correct answer is D (A sliding fifth wheel that can move forward and back along mounting rails): A sliding fifth wheel rides on mounting rails that let the entire assembly move forward and back on the tractor frame, which repositions the kingpin relative to the steer and drive axles and shifts weight distribution as needed for different loads. A fixed fifth wheel is bolted in one position and offers no such adjustment at all. A cab suspension system controls how the cab itself rides on the frame, and a landing gear gearbox raises and lowers the trailer's support legs, neither of which has any bearing on tractor axle weight distribution.
  147. The correct answer is C (The slide rails and their locking pins that hold the assembly): The slide rails allow the fifth wheel to be repositioned for weight distribution, while the locking pins hold the assembly securely in whichever position the driver has selected for the current load. If these pins are worn, damaged, or not fully engaged, the entire fifth wheel assembly can shift unexpectedly while the truck is underway, which seriously affects handling and weight distribution. The tilt cab cylinder and prop relate to raising the cab for engine service access, the seven pin connector carries electrical circuits, and the trailer height control valve manages suspension air pressure, none of which govern fifth wheel slide position.
  148. The correct answer is A (The release handle, which is linked mechanically to the locking jaws inside the fifth wheel): The release handle connects through a mechanical linkage directly to the locking jaws, so pulling it withdraws the jaws from around the kingpin and frees the trailer to separate from the tractor. The landing gear crank raises and lowers the trailer's own support legs and plays no role in the coupling mechanism itself. The height control valve adjusts cab or trailer ride height and has nothing to do with releasing the fifth wheel. The supply line glad hand only carries air to the trailer's air system and does not control the coupling jaws.
  149. The correct answer is C (Investigate and correct the binding, since a stuck linkage can prevent proper jaw release or full jaw closure): A release linkage must move freely because a stuck or binding mechanism can leave the jaws only partially closed around the kingpin or unable to release fully when needed, either of which is a real safety hazard. Replacing the entire top plate is an unnecessary and costly overcorrection when the linkage itself is the likely fault. Telling the driver to simply force the handle risks bending or breaking the linkage and does not fix the underlying binding. A jaw that closed correctly on the last attempt does not guarantee the binding will not cause a partial or failed release on a future attempt.
  150. The correct answer is B (A 2 inch diameter kingpin, which is the standard size used on most typical highway trailers): Most highway trailers are equipped with a standardized 2 inch diameter kingpin that is specifically designed to mate with the standard fifth wheel jaw opening found on the vast majority of highway tractors in North America. A 3.5 inch diameter kingpin exists as a separate standard used mainly on heavier specialized applications, but it is not the typical highway trailer size. A 1 inch kingpin is far too small for any standard highway coupling, and a 6 inch or 4 inch kingpin would not fit a conventional highway fifth wheel at all.
  151. The correct answer is C (Repeated coupling stress applied to the pin over an extended period of in service): Kingpins endure repeated coupling stress every time a tractor backs under and locks onto a trailer, and this cyclic loading over years of service can gradually wear the pin from its original round shape into an oval profile, a condition referred to as elongation. Tire inflation pressure, the trailer's ABS control module, and supply line air pressure are all unrelated mechanical stresses that do not act directly on the kingpin shank in this way. Elongation specifically results from the repeated mechanical loading the coupling process places on the pin over its service life.
  152. The correct answer is B (Wear, bending, or elongation present in the trailer's own kingpin rather): A worn, bent, or elongated kingpin will not seat correctly inside the jaws regardless of how well maintained the fifth wheel itself is, and this is described as a common root cause of coupling problems that drivers may mistakenly blame entirely on the tractor's fifth wheel. Checking the kingpin condition is therefore a logical early diagnostic step before condemning otherwise properly functioning fifth wheel hardware. Mud flap brackets, turn signal bulbs, and spare tire tread depth have no bearing whatsoever on the mechanical coupling process between kingpin and jaws.
  153. The correct answer is A (At the corners of the plate and around the bolts that secure it to the trailer frame): The upper coupler plate absorbs enormous stress during every coupling, uncoupling, and normal operating cycle, and that stress concentrates at the corners of the plate and around the mounting bolt holes, making those the locations where fatigue cracks most commonly begin. The trailer's air reservoir is an unrelated pressure vessel with no connection to the coupler plate. Cracking rarely starts along a plain geometric centreline with no stress-concentrating feature. The rear bumper mounting brackets are a completely separate structural component from the upper coupler plate.
  154. The correct answer is A (To support and hold the trailer level and stable whenever it is uncoupled): Landing gear consists of two vertical support legs that lower to the ground to support and keep the front of the trailer level and stable whenever it is not currently coupled to a tractor. It has no braking function whatsoever, plays no role in adjusting fifth wheel height on the tractor, and does not participate in charging the trailer's air reservoirs, which is instead handled through the supply glad hand connection and the trailer's own onboard air system components.
  155. The correct answer is D (When raising or lowering the legs while there is still significant weight on them): The low ratio setting on a two speed landing gear gearbox provides increased mechanical advantage that makes it easier to raise or lower the legs while there is still meaningful weight resting on them, such as during actual coupling or uncoupling of a loaded trailer. The high ratio setting instead lets the driver quickly run the legs when there is little or no weight to move, saving time and physical effort. An illuminated ABS lamp and disconnecting the electrical connector have no bearing on which gear ratio a driver should select.
  156. The correct answer is D (A driver pulling the tractor away from the trailer before the landing gear was fully lowered): Bent or cracked landing gear legs commonly result from a driver pulling the tractor away from the trailer before the landing gear has been fully lowered and is bearing weight properly, which loads the legs at an angle they were never designed to support. Excess grease on the fifth wheel plate has no relationship to landing gear structural damage. Overinflated rear tires and a slow glad hand gasket leak are both unrelated to how the landing gear legs are loaded during coupling and uncoupling.
  157. The correct answer is A (Because the bent leg may not reliably support the trailer's weight and could fail suddenly): A bent landing gear leg has compromised structural integrity and may not reliably continue supporting the trailer's substantial weight once it is uncoupled, creating a real risk of sudden and unpredictable failure at any time. This bending has no effect on spring brake release behaviour, no relationship to kingpin elongation, and no connection to the electrical turn signal circuits, all of which are entirely separate mechanical and electrical systems located elsewhere on the trailer.
  158. The correct answer is B (That the handle engages and disengages properly from the landing gear's internal gearbox mechanism): The crank handle must engage and disengage cleanly and reliably from the landing gear's internal gearbox so the driver can consistently raise and lower the support legs whenever needed. The handle's paint colour is a purely cosmetic detail with no bearing on its mechanical function. As a purely mechanical component, the crank handle has no electrical connection to the seven pin connector and no pneumatic connection whatsoever to the service brake air lines running elsewhere on the vehicle.
  159. The correct answer is C (Reduced stability and uneven support for the trailer's front end resting on those worn foot pads): Worn foot pads no longer present a flat, stable contact surface against the ground, so the trailer's front end can rock or settle unevenly while uncoupled, which is a real stability and safety concern during loading or maintenance. This wear has no direct electrical connection to the ABS control module, no relationship to the service brake air line's pressure integrity, and no direct mechanical connection to the tractor's fifth wheel locking jaws, which is a separate component entirely.
  160. The correct answer is A (Grinding noise and rough operation during cranking, which indicates a developing internal gearbox problem): Grinding or rough operation felt while cranking the landing gear indicates internal gearbox wear, physical damage, or a lack of adequate lubrication, and this symptom should be investigated promptly before it progresses into a complete gearbox failure that leaves the legs unable to be raised or lowered at all. Smooth resistance and a normal film of visible grease are both signs of properly functioning, well maintained equipment rather than problems. Needing two hands to operate a high ratio crank setting is not, by itself, evidence of an actual mechanical defect.
  161. The correct answer is D (A service line and a supply line, which apply the trailer brakes): The service line carries modulated air pressure that applies the trailer's brakes whenever the driver presses the brake pedal, while the supply line, also called the emergency line, continuously charges the trailer's air reservoirs and holds its spring brakes in the released position. Vacuum assist, engine coolant, hydraulic steering assist, differential lock, fuel transfer, and washer fluid lines are not part of the tractor to trailer air brake connection made through the glad hand fittings at all.
  162. The correct answer is B (The trailer's spring brakes automatically apply as a fail safe design feature built): A total loss of supply line pressure is specifically designed to cause the trailer's spring brakes to apply automatically, since these particular brakes are held in the released position only by continuous air pressure, and spring force applies them the instant that pressure is lost, a fail safe intended to prevent an uncontrolled trailer from rolling away. The landing gear, the fifth wheel's locking jaws, and the trailer's lighting circuits are all mechanically or electrically independent of the supply line's actual air pressure state.
  163. The correct answer is C (The seven pin connector for signs of corrosion, bent pins, or trapped moisture inside): A poor electrical connection at the seven pin connector, caused by corrosion, bent pins, or moisture intrusion, is a very common cause of an illuminated ABS lamp and should always be checked before assuming a wheel speed sensor or the electronic control module has actually failed. Only after confirming the connection is clean and properly seated does the technician move on to checking sensor resistance and pulling diagnostic trouble codes. Landing gear lubrication, fifth wheel grease, and kingpin clearance have no relationship whatsoever to this electrical ABS circuit.
  164. The correct answer is D (Check wheel speed sensor resistance and air gap, then pull diagnostic trouble codes): Once the electrical connection itself has been confirmed clean and properly seated, the correct next diagnostic step is to check the wheel speed sensor's resistance and physical air gap, followed by pulling diagnostic trouble codes using a scan tool to precisely isolate the actual underlying fault. Replacing the control unit before completing this diagnostic sequence risks unnecessary parts cost without confirming the true cause. Bleeding the reservoirs down and deliberately raising supply pressure beyond its normal range are not recognized diagnostic steps for this type of electrical ABS fault.
  165. The correct answer is D (Blue, the colour conventionally assigned to the service glad hand fitting): By long standing convention, the service glad hand is typically coloured blue while the supply glad hand is typically coloured red, giving technicians and drivers a quick visual reference for identifying each line. However, a technician should always confirm proper connection based on actual function and physical markings rather than relying on colour alone, especially when working on older or non standard equipment. Yellow and green are not the standard colours conventionally used for either of these two specific air line connections.
  166. The correct answer is C (Because older or non standard equipment may not consistently follow the conventional colour coding scheme): While service is conventionally coloured blue and supply is conventionally coloured red, older equipment or certain non standard aftermarket hardware may not consistently follow this convention, so confirming the actual function and any physical markings present helps avoid accidentally miscoupling the two lines. Colour coding is in fact widely used across the industry, so it is not absent, the two glad hands are not genuinely interchangeable since crossing them causes real functional brake problems, and colour coding itself is not prohibited by any inspection standard.
  167. The correct answer is C (It causes air leaks that can lead to slow pressure buildup or inconsistent trailer braking): A cracked, hardened, or otherwise missing glad hand gasket allows air to leak from the connection point, which can cause slow pressure buildup inside the trailer's reservoirs, inconsistent trailer braking performance, or in severe cases an inability to fully release the spring brakes as intended. This gasket condition has no effect on the tractor's fifth wheel locking jaws, does not change any published kingpin clearance specification, and a degraded gasket degrades sealing performance rather than improving it under any temperature condition.
  168. The correct answer is B (Any air leak causing a measurable pressure loss over the officially specified test period): Given the direct and serious safety implications of air brake system function, any air leak at a glad hand connection that causes a measurable pressure loss over the officially specified test period is typically treated as an out of service condition requiring immediate correction. A slightly different shade of colour, a reasonably routed line along the frame rail, or a modest length difference between the two lines are not themselves out of service defects unless they create an actual functional or genuine safety problem.
  169. The correct answer is B (A dedicated circuit that powers the trailer's ABS control unit and its malfunction indicator): On modern trailers, the seven pin connector also carries a dedicated circuit that powers the trailer's ABS control unit and its malfunction lamp, or alternatively feeds a matching warning indicator mounted inside the tractor's own cab for the driver to see. Engine coolant temperature signaling, fifth wheel hydraulic release, and fuel level sensing are not functions carried through this particular electrical connector linking the tractor and trailer together.
  170. The correct answer is D (The excessive tension created during a sharp turn can pull the connection loose): Hoses and cables routed too tightly can stretch excessively during sharp turning maneuvers, and this tension can pull the glad hand fitting or electrical connector loose from its mating half, creating a sudden and unexpected loss of air pressure or electrical continuity between the two units. Proper routing avoids both this kind of excessive tension and excessive slack that could drag or catch on other components. This particular routing issue has no effect on ABS sensor accuracy, fifth wheel plate wear, or kingpin clearance specifications.
  171. The correct answer is D (They can drag along the ground or catch on other nearby components during normal): Excessive slack in the routing of these hoses and cables allows them to hang low enough to drag along the ground or road surface during operation, or to catch on other chassis or trailer components while the vehicle is turning or maneuvering, risking physical damage or an unplanned disconnection. This particular slack issue has no relationship to a false coupling occurring at the fifth wheel, to the landing gear crank mechanism seizing, or to the kingpin's inherent resistance to elongation wear.
  172. The correct answer is C (Clean or replace the corroded connector first, then recheck whether the malfunction lamp clears before proceeding): Since corrosion found at the seven pin connector is a very common and easily correctable cause of an illuminated ABS lamp, the logical next step is to clean or replace the corroded connector and then recheck whether the lamp actually clears before moving on to any more invasive or expensive diagnostic work. Replacing sensors on every trailer axle without first ruling out the connector wastes both time and unnecessary parts cost. Raising supply pressure has no bearing on an electrical fault, and permanently disconnecting spring brakes would create a genuinely unsafe, uncontrolled trailer.
  173. The correct answer is C (It allows the two axles to move somewhat independently over uneven terrain while still sharing): A walking beam suspension connects two axles through a central pivot, allowing them to move somewhat independently as each one encounters uneven terrain, while still effectively sharing the overall load carried between the pair of axles. It does not provide any independent steering capability for the trailer's own axles, does not adjust kingpin height in any way, and the height control valve statement specifically applies to air ride systems rather than to mechanical walking beam designs, which instead rely on leaf springs.
  174. The correct answer is D (Periodic lubrication of the pivot bushings along with regular inspection of the leaves for cracks): Walking beam suspensions are valued for their durability and mechanical simplicity, needing relatively little ongoing maintenance beyond periodically lubricating the central pivot bushings and regularly inspecting the leaf springs themselves for any cracks or outright breaks developing over time. Fifth wheel grease, ABS control unit calibration, and landing gear gearbox ratio adjustment are all unrelated maintenance tasks that are instead tied to entirely different trailer systems located elsewhere on the vehicle.
  175. The correct answer is B (It automatically adjusts air pressure inside the air springs to maintain a consistent, correct ride): The height control valve on an air ride suspension continuously senses the actual distance between the axle and the trailer frame, and automatically adjusts air pressure inside the springs to maintain a consistent, correct ride height as the trailer's load varies from empty all the way up to fully loaded. It has no function locking the landing gear in place, no role releasing the spring brakes under any load condition, and no effect whatsoever on kingpin to jaw clearance, which is an entirely separate mechanical system.
  176. The correct answer is D (Driveline or suspension component interference caused by the abnormally low riding height of the trailer): If the height control valve is misadjusted so the trailer sits too low, various components such as the driveline or other suspension parts can begin interfering with each other or with the trailer frame itself, causing physical damage or accelerated abnormal wear over time. This particular misadjustment does not release the spring brakes on its own, does not affect elongation happening inside the fifth wheel jaws, and has no effect whatsoever on the kingpin's actual physical diameter.
  177. The correct answer is D (It can negatively affect the geometry needed for proper coupling as well as overall vehicle stability): A trailer riding too high due to a misadjusted height control valve can negatively affect the geometry required for proper coupling to a tractor's fifth wheel and can also affect overall vehicle handling stability during operation. This particular condition has no direct effect on the seven pin connector's electrical function, does not itself change any published kingpin clearance specification, and the landing gear's foot pads are not in ground contact at all while the legs remain fully retracted for highway travel.
  178. The correct answer is A (Cracked or sagging springs, worn pivot bushings, and loose or missing U bolts securing the axle): Regardless of the specific leaf spring configuration used on a given trailer, this portion of the inspection includes checking for cracked or sagging springs, worn pivot bushings, and loose or missing U bolts, all of which compromise the suspension's ability to properly support and control the axle underneath the trailer. The seven pin connector, the fifth wheel's release handle, and the tractor cab's tilt hydraulic system are entirely different systems located elsewhere on the combination vehicle, unrelated to trailer spring suspension defects.
  179. The correct answer is C (Conduct a closer, more detailed inspection of the trailer suspension system even before taking any): An uneven, low riding trailer observed by eye is described as a visible red flag that should prompt a closer, more detailed suspension inspection even before any formal measurement is actually taken, since this appearance often indicates a broken spring, an air leak, or a failed height control valve. This particular observation points toward the trailer's own suspension rather than toward the electrical connector or the tractor's fifth wheel jaws, and dismissing such a clear visible red flag would ignore a legitimate and useful early warning sign.
  180. The correct answer is C (Trailer suspension components can wear differently, and sometimes less predictably, compared with a tractor's own suspension): Because trailers experience varied coupling histories across different tractors and often endure extended static loaded periods parked between trips, their suspension components can wear differently, and sometimes less predictably, than a tractor's own suspension does, which is exactly why a thorough and consistent inspection routine matters just as much on the trailer side of the fleet. This does not mean trailer suspensions need no inspection at all, that wear is identical across an entire fleet, or that lubrication is never required under any circumstance, all of which contradict standard maintenance practice.
  181. The correct answer is A (That the mechanism engages properly and cannot be released without deliberate, intentional action taken): Inspectors confirm that the fifth wheel's locking mechanism actually engages properly and, critically, cannot be released accidentally, only through deliberate, intentional action taken by the driver at the release handle, since an accidental release while the vehicle is underway on the highway would be genuinely catastrophic. Paint colour is a purely cosmetic detail and irrelevant to this safety check, the mechanism is fundamentally mechanical rather than hydraulically operated in a standard fifth wheel design, and the fifth wheel itself is mounted on the tractor frame rather than anywhere near the trailer's rear axle.
  182. The correct answer is C (Any visible evidence of the cab actually shifting on its mounts relative to the frame underneath): Inspectors confirm the cab is securely mounted with no missing or broken bolts and, importantly, no visible evidence of shifting occurring on its mounts, since shifting indicates worn or already failing mounting hardware that could allow further movement or an eventual complete mount failure over time. The choice between rubber isolator mounts and a full air suspension system is simply a manufacturer design decision rather than a defect. The presence of a safety prop and a working height control valve are both genuinely required, correctly functioning features rather than conditions an inspector should be flagging as absent.
  183. The correct answer is A (Bolt torque values along with the overall structural condition of the brackets, including any visible): Inspection of the fifth wheel's mounting assembly includes checking bolt torque values along with the overall physical condition of the support brackets, including looking closely for any cracking present, since loose bolts or cracked brackets compromise the entire assembly's ability to safely transfer load between the tractor and the trailer under real world driving conditions. Hardware colour finish and a particular grease brand are simply cosmetic or product preference details rather than genuine structural safety checks, and trailer spare tire pressure is completely unrelated to fifth wheel mounting hardware integrity.
  184. The correct answer is A (Cracks, excessive wear, and elongation affecting both the kingpin itself and the surrounding upper coupler): Inspectors specifically look for cracks, excessive wear, and elongation affecting both the kingpin and the surrounding upper coupler plate together, since these particular defects directly threaten the structural integrity of the entire coupling connection joining the trailer to the tractor's fifth wheel. Colour finish or brand markings, the trailer's fuel tank capacity, and the total number of axles installed are not part of this specific structural inspection focus on the kingpin and upper coupler assembly.
  185. The correct answer is B (That the landing gear locks securely in the fully raised position appropriate for highway travel): Inspectors confirm the landing gear locks securely in the fully raised position before the trailer is cleared to travel on the highway, since legs that are not properly locked upward can drop unexpectedly or drag along the road surface during transport, creating a serious and immediate road hazard for the driver and other motorists. Matching paint colour is purely cosmetic, the specific lubricant type used in the gearbox is a maintenance specification rather than a simple pass or fail inspection item, and whether the crank handle happens to be removable without tools has no bearing on safe operation.
  186. The correct answer is B (The glad hand gasket and the coupling itself, checking specifically for a restriction): Even with adequate pressure shown by a gauge located elsewhere in the system, a restriction, a leak, or a poor seal specifically at the glad hand gasket and coupling point can prevent the full supply pressure from actually reaching the trailer's individual spring brake chambers, keeping those brakes from releasing completely as intended. The turn signal wiring harness, the landing gear crank shaft bearing, and the fifth wheel release handle's return spring are unrelated mechanical or electrical components that play no role at all in delivering spring brake air supply.
  187. The correct answer is B (Both findings are genuinely serious defects that must be corrected before this trailer returns to active): Both a bent landing gear leg and a kingpin elongated beyond specification are genuinely serious defects that risk sudden structural failure and ongoing coupling problems respectively, so both conditions should be corrected before this trailer is returned to active service on the road. Landing gear failure and kingpin failure are each independently serious safety issues in their own right, rather than one being safety related while the other is merely cosmetic, and neither defect should wait on a specific driver request once a genuine safety issue has already been clearly identified.
  188. The correct answer is A (A properly maintained fifth wheel keeps tractor and trailer securely joined through braking, cornering, and highway): The fifth wheel is the coupling device responsible for keeping the entire tractor trailer combination physically joined together through all the dynamic forces produced by braking, cornering, and ordinary highway flexing, and its failure can allow the trailer to separate entirely from the tractor at highway speed, a genuinely catastrophic outcome for everyone nearby. It is certainly not the only vehicle component ever subject to inspection standards, its cost is not the actual reason for its recognized safety significance, and it is not described anywhere as requiring the least frequent inspection, quite the opposite given its clearly critical safety role.
  189. The correct answer is A (Small, seemingly minor defects like a worn kingpin or a cracked gasket can escalate into serious): The central theme worth emphasizing is that cabs and trailers involve mechanical systems where a small, seemingly minor defect, such as a worn kingpin, a cracked glad hand gasket, or a bent landing gear leg, can escalate into a genuinely serious safety failure, making careful and thorough inspection habits a direct line of defence for everyone sharing the road. There is no meaningful redundancy that makes such defects unimportant, electrical connections are not the only safety relevant systems discussed in this material, and these inspections are grounded in real safety consequences rather than mere paperwork compliance.
  190. The correct answer is D (That the fifth wheel's throat and jaws are actually designed and sized to accept that specific): A fifth wheel's throat and jaws are manufactured to accept a specific kingpin diameter, so a technician must confirm the fifth wheel installed on a given tractor is actually designed for the kingpin diameter present on the trailer being coupled, since mismatched sizes will not seat or lock correctly regardless of how well maintained either component otherwise is. Overall trailer length, landing gear gearbox ratio, and glad hand colour coding are all unrelated to whether a kingpin diameter is compatible with a specific fifth wheel's throat and jaw dimensions.
  191. The correct answer is D (The supply line, which is sometimes referred to by drivers as the emergency line): this line stays pressurized continuously, recharging the trailer reservoirs and holding the spring brakes released. If supply pressure drops or is lost entirely, the spring brakes apply automatically as a fail safe. The service line instead carries modulated pressure only when the pedal is pressed, and neither an auxiliary nor a bypass line exists in this trailer air system.
  192. The correct answer is B (Blue, matching the service circuit that applies pressure when the pedal is pressed): the service glad hand is conventionally coloured blue, while the supply or emergency glad hand is conventionally red. A technician should still confirm the correct connection by shape, marking, and actual function rather than colour alone, since older or non standard equipment may not follow this convention consistently. Green and yellow are not part of the recognized glad hand colour scheme.
  193. The correct answer is C (The condition of the rubber sealing gaskets seated inside each glad hand fitting): a cracked, hardened, or missing gasket is a common and easily checked cause of an audible air leak at the coupling, directly explaining slow release. Landing gear bolts, fifth wheel lubrication, and kingpin alignment have no relationship to an air leak located right at the nose box couplings. Checking the simple, external, low cost item first avoids needless teardown of internal trailer valves.
  194. The correct answer is A (Clean or replace the corroded connector before testing any further downstream components): a poor electrical connection at the seven pin connector is a very common and inexpensive cause of an illuminated ABS lamp, so it should be ruled out before assuming a costlier internal component has failed. Replacing the control unit or recalibrating sensors are invasive steps that should follow this basic check, not precede it. Bleeding brake chambers addresses air system moisture, not an electrical fault signalled by a lamp.
  195. The correct answer is C (Seven pins, a design used across most highway tractor and trailer combinations): the standard North American trailer connector is commonly a seven pin design with dedicated circuits for running lights, stop lights, turn signals, ground, auxiliary power, and the ABS circuit on modern trailers. A four pin connector is typically found on small light duty trailers rather than heavy commercial units. Nine and twelve pin connectors are not the recognized industry standard for this application.
  196. The correct answer is D (The ABS specific circuit within the shared connector housing has developed its own isolated fault): since running lights and turn signals share the connector housing but use separate wires and pins, a fault confined only to the ABS circuit points to a break, corrosion, or short specific to that conductor rather than a connector wide failure. Replacing the entire connector blind is inefficient. Spring brake supply pressure and a burned out dash bulb would not selectively cause only this ABS lamp behaviour.
  197. The correct answer is B (The wheel speed sensor resistance and the sensor's air gap against its tone ring): once the electrical connector has been ruled out as clean and properly seated, the next logical step is checking the sensors feeding data to the ABS control unit, since an incorrect air gap or damaged winding also triggers a fault. Landing gear chain tension, fifth wheel lubrication, and tire pressure are unrelated to ABS wheel speed signal generation, and codes would only be pulled after these mechanical checks.
  198. The correct answer is A (To prevent an uncontrolled trailer from rolling away if the air supply is ever lost): this fail safe design ensures any interruption in supply pressure, whether from a broken line, a disconnected glad hand, or a system failure, applies the spring brakes automatically rather than releasing them. It has no relationship to fuel economy, landing gear operation, or connector temperature, and this principle explains why the supply line is treated as a critical safety item during every inspection.
  199.
